subtopics.subtitle: V = IR and its limits, resistance and resistivity, conductance, temperature effect on R

concepts.text: Ohm's Law

Ohm's Law states that the current flowing through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage across the two points, provided the temperature and other physical conditions remain constant. Equivalently, current is directly proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance, and the ratio V/I is a constant called the resistance R. Here V is voltage in volts, I is current in amperes and R is resistance in ohms; any one quantity can be found when the other two are known.

concepts.plainText: V = I × R

concepts.text: The three forms of the law:
items: V = I × R — voltage drop across a resistance R carrying current I
I = V / R — current drawn by a resistance R from a supply V
R = V / I — resistance found from a voltmeter and an ammeter reading
The V-I graph of an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin; with V on the vertical axis its slope equals R

concepts.text: Limitations: Ohm's law holds only for ohmic (linear) conductors kept at constant temperature, such as metals and carbon resistors. It fails for non-ohmic devices whose V-I curve is not a straight line — semiconductor diodes and transistors, thermistors, vacuum tubes, electrolytes and gas-discharge lamps. Even a metal filament lamp departs from it because its temperature, and hence its resistance, rises with the current. Unilateral elements such as diodes break the law in a second way: their resistance depends on the direction of the current.

rows: Metallic conductors, wire-wound and carbon resistors
Diodes, transistors, thermistors, arc and discharge lamps
V-I graph: straight line through the origin
V-I graph: curved, may differ for each direction
R constant at a fixed temperature
R changes with V, I or current direction

concepts.text: Resistance, Resistivity and Conductance

The resistance of a conductor depends on its material, length and cross-sectional area. It is directly proportional to the length l and inversely proportional to the area A; the constant of proportionality ρ (rho) is the resistivity or specific resistance of the material — numerically the resistance between opposite faces of a 1 m cube of it, so its unit is the ohm-metre (Ω·m).

concepts.plainText: R = ρ × l / A

concepts.text: Key facts:
items: Resistivity (ρ) is a material property, measured in ohm-metres; copper ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m.
Doubling the length doubles the resistance.
Doubling the cross-sectional area halves the resistance; doubling the diameter quarters it, because A ∝ d².
Stretching a wire to n times its length at constant volume shrinks A to A/n, so R rises n² times.
For metals, resistance increases with temperature (positive temperature coefficient).

concepts.text: Conductance G is the reciprocal of resistance and measures how easily current flows: G = 1/R = I/V, with SI unit the siemens (S), formerly called the mho. Conductivity σ (sigma) is the reciprocal of resistivity, σ = 1/ρ, measured in siemens per metre (S/m); for a conductor G = σA/l. Copper has σ ≈ 5.8 × 10⁷ S/m, one of the highest values of any metal. Conductances of parallel branches add directly, which makes G convenient for parallel circuits.
Effect of Temperature on Resistance

The resistance of a pure metal rises almost linearly with temperature because the vibrating lattice ions scatter the free electrons more strongly. If R₀ is the resistance at 0 °C and α₀ the temperature coefficient of resistance at 0 °C (in per °C), the resistance at t °C is R_t = R₀(1 + α₀t). Between any two temperatures t₁ and t₂ the resistances are related by R₂ = R₁[1 + α₁(t₂ − t₁)], where α₁ is the coefficient at t₁; the coefficient itself falls with temperature, α_t = α₀/(1 + α₀t). Copper has α₀ ≈ 0.00427/°C (0.00393/°C at 20 °C), so its resistance grows by roughly 0.4% per degree.

concepts.plainText: R_t = R₀ (1 + α₀ t)

concepts.text: Sign of the temperature coefficient:
items: Pure metals: positive — copper ≈ 0.004/°C, aluminium ≈ 0.004/°C, tungsten ≈ 0.0045/°C.
Alloys such as manganin, constantan and eureka: almost zero — used for standard resistors and meter shunts.
Semiconductors, insulators, carbon and electrolytes: negative — resistance falls as temperature rises (the thermistor principle).

concepts.text: Worked example: a copper field coil has a resistance of 50 Ω at 20 °C. Its resistance at 70 °C, taking α₂₀ = 0.00393/°C, is R₂ = 50 × [1 + 0.00393 × (70 − 20)] = 50 × 1.1965 ≈ 59.8 Ω. Connected to a 230 V supply the coil draws I = 230/59.8 ≈ 3.85 A when hot, compared with 230/50 = 4.6 A when cold — Ohm's law must be applied with the resistance at the actual operating temperature.
Going Deeper: Ohm's Law and Resistance

Ohm's law has a microscopic form that explains where resistance comes from. Inside a conductor an electric field E drives a current density J (current per unit area), and for an ohmic material the two are proportional, J = σE. For a uniform wire of length l and area A the field is E = V/l and the current is I = JA, so I = σAV/l. Rearranged this is V = I × l/(σA), which is exactly V = IR with R = ρl/A. Resistance is therefore just conductivity scaled by the wire's geometry.

concepts.plainText: J = I/A = σE, so R = l/(σA) = ρl/A

concepts.text: For a non-ohmic device the ratio V/I changes from point to point on its characteristic. The value of V/I at a chosen operating point is called the static or DC resistance, while the slope ΔV/ΔI of the curve at that point is the dynamic or AC resistance. For an ohmic resistor the two are equal and constant; for a forward-biased diode the dynamic resistance is much smaller than the static value.

rows: Stretched to n times length (same volume)
Cut into n equal parts joined in parallel
each part R/n, n in parallel
Same material and mass, length × n

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - resistance of a line at working temperature
Aluminium wire: l = 2 km, d = 3 mm, rho(20 C) = 2.8e-8 ohm-m, alpha20 = 0.0039 /C
Step 1: A = pi d^2 / 4 = pi x (3e-3)^2 / 4 = 7.069e-6 m^2
Step 2: R20 = rho l / A = 2.8e-8 x 2000 / 7.069e-6 = 7.92 ohm
Step 3: R50 = R20 [1 + alpha20 (50 - 20)] = 7.92 x 1.117 = 8.85 ohm
Step 4: current from a 24 V source at 50 C: I = 24 / 8.85 = 2.71 A
Check: forgetting the /4 in the area would give R 4 times too small.

Because the resistance of a pure metal falls almost linearly as it is cooled, the straight line extended backwards meets zero resistance at a temperature −T, where T = 1/α₀. For copper T ≈ 234.5 °C. The resistances at any two temperatures are then in the ratio of their distances from −T, which avoids having to convert α from one reference temperature to another.

concepts.plainText: R₂/R₁ = (T + t₂)/(T + t₁), T = 1/α₀ ≈ 234.5 for copper

concepts.text:
Worked example 2 - finding temperature from resistance
A copper coil measures 30 ohm at 15 C and 35 ohm after running. alpha0 = 0.00427 /C
Step 1: R0 = R15 / (1 + alpha0 x 15) = 30 / 1.06405 = 28.19 ohm
Step 2: Rt = R0 (1 + alpha0 t)  ->  t = (Rt/R0 - 1) / alpha0
Step 3: t = (35 / 28.19 - 1) / 0.00427 = 0.2414 / 0.00427 = 56.5 C
Cross-check with T = 1/alpha0 = 234.2: t2 = (35/30)(234.2 + 15) - 234.2 = 56.5 C
Temperature rise = 56.5 - 15 = 41.5 C

A series combination of a positive-coefficient conductor and a negative-coefficient one can be made almost temperature independent. The change in total resistance for a small temperature rise Δt is (R₁α₁ + R₂α₂)Δt, so it vanishes when R₁α₁ = −R₂α₂. For example, 2 Ω of copper (α ≈ 0.0043/°C) needs 2 × 0.0043/0.0005 = 17.2 Ω of carbon (α ≈ −0.0005/°C) in series.
Common mistakes in resistance problems:
items: Using the diameter in place of the radius in A = πr², which makes the area four times too large.
Leaving the area in mm² or cm² instead of converting to m² (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m²).
Applying α₀ to a resistance measured at 20 °C; use α₂₀, the two-temperature formula or first find R₀.
Treating resistivity as if it depended on the length or area of the sample; it depends only on the material and its temperature.
Assuming a stretched wire only gets longer; at constant volume its area falls too, so R rises as the square of the stretch.

concepts.text: For stretch, cut-and-parallel and same-mass questions, work with ratios rather than actual values: write R ∝ l/A, express the new l and A as multiples of the old, and the answer usually drops out as n or n².

notes.text: Power questions usually hide Ohm's law inside: memorize all three forms P = VI, I²R and V²/R so you can pick the one matching the given quantities.
Ohm's law applies to ohmic (linear) devices only — not to diodes, thermistors, or filament lamps at varying temperature.
A 'short circuit' has R ≈ 0 (V ≈ 0 across it); an 'open circuit' has R = infinity (I = 0 through it).

Unit traps: resistivity is in Ω·m (not Ω/m), conductance in siemens (S), conductivity in S/m and the temperature coefficient α in per °C. When a question gives R at 0 °C use α₀ directly; when it gives R at 20 °C use α₂₀ (0.00393/°C for copper) or the two-temperature formula.

formulas.title: Ohm's law
formulas.description: V in volts, I in amperes, R in ohms; valid for ohmic conductors at constant temperature.

formulas.title: Resistance of a conductor
formulas.description: ρ = resistivity (Ω·m), l = length (m), A = cross-sectional area (m²); use for wires, cables and heating elements.

formulas.title: Conductance and conductivity
formulas.description: G in siemens (S), σ in S/m; conductances of parallel branches add directly.

formulas.title: Resistance at temperature t
formulas.description: R₀ = resistance at 0 °C, α₀ = temperature coefficient at 0 °C (per °C), t in °C; α₀ is positive for metals.

formulas.title: Resistance between two temperatures
formulas.description: Use when the known resistance R₁ is at a temperature t₁ other than 0 °C; α₁ is the coefficient at t₁.

formulas.title: Temperature coefficient at t
formulas.description: Converts the 0 °C coefficient to its value at t °C; for copper 0.00427 at 0 °C becomes 0.00393 at 20 °C.

flashcards.front: State Ohm's law and the condition under which it holds.
flashcards.back: At constant temperature the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it: V = IR. It applies only to ohmic (linear) conductors.

flashcards.front: A wire is stretched to twice its length (volume constant). How does its resistance change?
flashcards.back: Length doubles and area halves, so R = ρl/A becomes 4 times the original.

flashcards.front: What are the units of conductance and conductivity?
flashcards.back: Conductance G = 1/R is in siemens (S, formerly mho); conductivity σ = 1/ρ is in siemens per metre (S/m).

flashcards.front: Which materials have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance?
flashcards.back: Semiconductors, insulators, carbon and electrolytes — their resistance falls as temperature rises. Pure metals have a positive coefficient; alloys like manganin are nearly zero.

questions.questionText: A heating element of resistance 46 Ω is connected to a 230 V supply. The current it draws is:
A current of 2.5 mA flows through a 4.7 kΩ resistor. The voltage across the resistor is:
On the V-I graph of an ohmic conductor, with voltage V on the vertical axis and current I on the horizontal axis, the slope of the straight line represents:
questions.explanation: Slope = ΔV/ΔI = R. If the axes were swapped (I vertical) the slope would be the conductance 1/R.

questions.questionText: Ohm's law cannot be applied directly to which of the following?
options: A copper wire at constant temperature
questions.explanation: A diode is non-linear and unilateral: its V/I ratio changes with the applied voltage and with polarity, so it is non-ohmic. The others are ohmic conductors.

questions.questionText: The SI unit of resistivity is:
questions.explanation: From ρ = RA/l the unit is Ω × m²/m = Ω·m. S/m is the unit of conductivity, the reciprocal of resistivity.

questions.questionText: For a metal wire kept at constant temperature, which of the following does NOT change its resistance?
options: The material it is made of
questions.explanation: R = ρl/A depends on material (ρ), length and area. For an ohmic conductor the current simply changes in proportion to the voltage, so V/I stays the same.

questions.questionText: The conductance of a 25 Ω resistor is:
The SI unit of conductivity σ is:
questions.explanation: σ = 1/ρ, so its unit is 1/(Ω·m) = S/m. The siemens alone is the unit of conductance.

questions.questionText: When the temperature of a pure metal conductor rises, its resistance:
questions.explanation: Pure metals have a positive temperature coefficient: stronger lattice vibration scatters the free electrons more, so resistance rises.

questions.questionText: Which material is most suitable for precision standard resistors because its resistance hardly changes with temperature?
questions.explanation: Manganin (a copper-manganese-nickel alloy) has a temperature coefficient close to zero. Copper and tungsten have large positive coefficients and carbon has a negative one.

questions.questionText: An open circuit between two points has:
options: Zero resistance and zero voltage across it
Zero resistance and a very large current
Infinite resistance and zero current through it
Infinite resistance and maximum current through it
questions.explanation: An open circuit is a break in the path: R → ∞, so I = V/R = 0 even though a voltage may appear across the gap. Zero resistance describes a short circuit.

questions.questionText: The diameter of a wire is doubled while its length and material stay the same. Its new resistance, in terms of the original resistance R, is:
questions.explanation: A = πd²/4, so doubling d makes the area four times larger and R = ρl/A becomes one-quarter.

questions.questionText: Ohm's law, V ∝ I, holds for a metallic conductor provided that:
options: Its temperature and other physical conditions remain constant
The conductor is made of an alloy
questions.explanation: The proportionality between V and I holds only while the physical state, chiefly the temperature, of the conductor is unchanged.

questions.questionText: A resistor draws 2 A from a 12 V supply. If the supply is raised to 18 V and the resistance stays the same, the current becomes:
questions.explanation: R = 12/2 = 6 Ω, so I = 18/6 = 3 A; the current rises in the same ratio as the voltage.

questions.questionText: A copper conductor is 100 m long with a cross-sectional area of 1 mm². Taking ρ = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, its resistance is:
A nichrome wire (ρ = 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m) is 10 m long and 0.5 mm in diameter. Its resistance is approximately:
A wire of resistance 4 Ω is drawn out until its length is three times the original, its volume remaining constant. Its new resistance is:
questions.explanation: Length × 3 and area ÷ 3, so R = ρl/A rises 3 × 3 = 9 times: 4 × 9 = 36 Ω.

questions.questionText: A carbon resistor carries the colour bands yellow, violet, red and gold. The range within which its actual resistance may lie is:
questions.explanation: Yellow = 4, violet = 7, red = ×100, so the nominal value is 47 × 100 = 4.7 kΩ; gold means ±5 %, giving 4.7 kΩ ± 235 Ω = 4.465 kΩ to 4.935 kΩ. The first option wrongly uses ±10 % (silver).

questions.questionText: Two wires of the same material and length have diameters in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of their resistances R₁ : R₂ is:
questions.explanation: R ∝ 1/A ∝ 1/d², so R₁/R₂ = (d₂/d₁)² = 2² = 4, i.e. 4 : 1.

questions.questionText: Two wires are made from the same material and have equal mass. Their lengths are in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of their resistances R₁ : R₂ is:
questions.explanation: For fixed mass (fixed volume) A = volume/l, so R = ρl/A = ρl²/volume ∝ l². R₁/R₂ = (1/2)² = 1/4.

questions.questionText: A copper tube 2 m long has an outer diameter of 10 mm and an inner diameter of 8 mm. Taking ρ = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, its resistance from end to end is about:
questions.explanation: Only the metal ring carries current: A = π(D² − d²)/4 = π(100 − 64)/4 = 28.3 mm², so R = ρl/A = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ × 2/(28.3 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 1.22 mΩ. Using the outer or inner circle alone gives 0.438 mΩ or 0.684 mΩ.

questions.questionText: The temperature coefficient of resistance of a metal at 0 °C is 0.004 /°C. Assuming it stays constant, at what temperature will the resistance of the metal be double its value at 0 °C?
A copper winding has a resistance of 10 Ω at 25 °C. Using the inferred zero-resistance temperature of copper, −234.5 °C, its resistance at 75 °C is:
Which of the following statements about resistivity is NOT correct?
options: It is a property of the material of the conductor
Its SI unit is the ohm-metre
It doubles when the length of the wire is doubled
For a metal it increases as the temperature rises
questions.explanation: Resistivity is a material constant at a given temperature; doubling the length doubles the resistance R, not the resistivity ρ.

questions.questionText: The resistance of carbon or a pure semiconductor falls as its temperature rises mainly because:
options: More charge carriers are freed, and this outweighs the increased scattering
The material expands and its area increases
The free electrons stop colliding with the lattice
questions.explanation: Heating breaks more covalent bonds, so the carrier concentration rises steeply; this effect dominates the extra lattice scattering, giving a negative temperature coefficient.

questions.questionText: The resistance of a metallic conductor increases with temperature because:
options: The number of free electrons falls sharply
The conductor contracts and its area decreases
The charge on each electron increases
Stronger lattice vibrations scatter the free electrons more often
questions.explanation: In a metal the free-electron density is practically fixed; heating increases the vibration of the lattice ions, which shortens the time between collisions and reduces the drift for a given field.

questions.questionText: A copper conductor (σ = 5.8 × 10⁷ S/m) carries a uniform electric field of 0.01 V/m. The current density in it is:
questions.explanation: Microscopic Ohm's law: J = σE = 5.8 × 10⁷ × 0.01 = 5.8 × 10⁵ A/m².

questions.questionText: A conductor with a cross-sectional area of 2.5 mm² carries a current of 10 A. The current density is:
The resistance of a tungsten filament lamp measured cold with an ohmmeter, compared with the value V²/P calculated from its rating, is:
questions.explanation: Tungsten has a large positive temperature coefficient; the filament runs at about 2500 °C, so its hot resistance is roughly 10 to 15 times the cold value. This is why a lamp draws a surge of current when switched on.

questions.questionText: For a non-linear device, the ratio V/I at a particular operating point on its characteristic is called its:
questions.explanation: V/I at a point is the static resistance; the slope ΔV/ΔI at that point is the dynamic resistance. The two are equal only for an ohmic element.

questions.questionText: Three resistors with conductances 0.2 S, 0.05 S and 0.25 S are connected in parallel across a 10 V supply. The total current drawn is:
questions.explanation: Parallel conductances add: G = 0.2 + 0.05 + 0.25 = 0.5 S, so I = GV = 0.5 × 10 = 5 A.

questions.questionText: A wire 2 m long with a cross-sectional area of 1 mm² has a resistance of 0.04 Ω. The conductivity of its material is:
A wire is stretched so that its length increases by 10%, its volume remaining constant. Its resistance increases by:
questions.explanation: Length × 1.1 and area ÷ 1.1, so R × 1.1² = 1.21, an increase of 21%.

questions.questionText: The resistance of a circuit increases by 25% while the applied voltage is kept constant. The current decreases by:
questions.explanation: I ∝ 1/R, so I_new = I/1.25 = 0.8I; the current falls by 20%, not 25%.

questions.questionText: Wires A and B are made of the same material. A is twice as long as B and has three times the diameter of B. The ratio R_A/R_B is:
Which of the following statements about conductance is NOT correct?
options: Conductances connected in series add directly
Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance
Its SI unit is the siemens, formerly the mho
Conductances connected in parallel add directly
questions.explanation: In parallel, G_total = G₁ + G₂ + …; in series it is the resistances that add, so 1/G_total = 1/G₁ + 1/G₂ + ….

questions.questionText: A copper wire is 500 m long and 2 mm in diameter. Taking ρ = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m at 20 °C and α₂₀ = 0.00393 /°C, its resistance at 60 °C is approximately:
A coil has a resistance of 20 Ω at 20 °C and 24 Ω at 70 °C. Its temperature coefficient of resistance referred to 0 °C (α₀) is approximately:
questions.explanation: 20 = R₀(1 + 20α₀) and 24 = R₀(1 + 70α₀). Dividing: 24 + 480α₀ = 20 + 1400α₀, so α₀ = 4/920 ≈ 0.00435 /°C (the value 0.004 is α₂₀, not α₀).

questions.questionText: The field winding of a machine has a resistance of 40 Ω at 20 °C. After a long run its resistance is 48 Ω. Taking α₂₀ = 0.00393 /°C for copper, the final temperature of the winding is approximately:

A 1 Ω copper resistor (α = +0.004 /°C) is to be connected in series with a carbon resistor (α = −0.0005 /°C) so that the total resistance does not change with small temperature changes. The carbon resistor should be:
questions.explanation: Zero net change requires R_Cu α_Cu = R_C |α_C|: 1 × 0.004 = R_C × 0.0005, so R_C = 8 Ω.

questions.questionText: A tungsten lamp filament has a resistance of 20 Ω at 20 °C. When lit it draws 0.5 A from a 120 V supply. Taking α₂₀ = 0.005 /°C and assuming it stays constant, the filament temperature is approximately:
A copper wire 1000 m long has a mass of 8.9 kg. Taking the density of copper as 8900 kg/m³ and ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, the resistance of the wire is:

A copper coil connected to a 110 V DC supply draws 5 A when switched on at a room temperature of 15 °C. After some hours the current has fallen to 4.4 A. Taking α₀ = 0.00427 /°C, the final temperature of the coil is approximately:
When the voltage across a fixed resistor is increased by 20 V, the current through it increases by 25%. The original voltage across the resistor was:
questions.explanation: R is constant, so V/I = (V + 20)/(1.25I) gives 1.25V = V + 20, so V = 80 V.

questions.questionText: A rectangular metal block measures 1 cm × 2 cm × 4 cm. The ratio of the largest to the smallest resistance that can be measured between a pair of opposite faces is:
questions.explanation: R_max = ρ(4)/(1 × 2) = 2ρ and R_min = ρ(1)/(2 × 4) = ρ/8 (lengths in cm), so the ratio is 2/(1/8) = 16.

questions.questionText: A load 50 m away from a supply is fed by a two-core copper cable, each core having a cross-section of 6 mm² (ρ = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m). When the load draws 20 A, the total voltage drop in the cable is approximately:
questions.explanation: The current flows out and back, so l = 100 m: R = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ × 100 / 6 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.287 Ω; drop = IR = 20 × 0.287 ≈ 5.73 V.

subtopics.title: Electric Voltage, Current, Power & Energy
subtopics.subtitle: Charge and current, EMF and p.d., the three power forms, energy in joules and kWh

concepts.text: Electric Charge and Current

Electric charge Q is measured in coulombs (C); one coulomb is the charge of about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons, each electron carrying 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Electric current is the rate of flow of charge through a conductor, I = Q/t, and one ampere is a flow of one coulomb per second. Conventional current is taken to flow from the positive terminal to the negative terminal outside the source, opposite to the actual direction of electron flow.

concepts.plainText: I = Q / t   (1 A = 1 C/s)

concepts.text: Types of current:
items: Direct current (DC): flows in one direction only with a steady magnitude — batteries, solar cells, rectifier outputs.
Alternating current (AC): reverses direction periodically; the Nepal mains is a 230 V, 50 Hz sinusoid.
Current is measured with an ammeter connected in series with the load (very low resistance).

concepts.text: Voltage, Potential Difference and EMF

Voltage is the electrical 'pressure' that pushes charge round a circuit. It is the work done per unit charge, V = W/Q, so one volt equals one joule per coulomb. Potential difference (p.d.) is the voltage between two points of a circuit — for example the drop across a resistor — and it exists only while current flows through resistance. Electromotive force (EMF) is the voltage that a source (cell, generator) develops internally to drive charge; it equals the terminal voltage only at no load. A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the two points (very high resistance).

concepts.plainText: V = W / Q   (1 V = 1 J/C)

rows: Produced by a source: cell, battery, generator
Exists between any two points of a circuit
Effect of current flowing through a resistance
Equals the terminal voltage only at no load
Terminal p.d. on load: V = E − I r
Always greater than or equal to terminal p.d.
Sum of p.d.s round a loop equals the EMF (KVL)

concepts.text: Electric Power and Energy

Power is the rate of doing work or of converting electrical energy, measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). For any element P = VI; combining this with Ohm's law gives P = I²R and P = V²/R for a resistor, where the power appears as heat (Joule heating). Larger units are the kilowatt (1 kW = 10³ W) and the megawatt (1 MW = 10⁶ W); motor outputs are still quoted in horsepower, 1 hp = 746 W (metric hp ≈ 735.5 W).

concepts.plainText: P = V × I = I² × R = V² / R

concepts.text: Energy is the total work done over a period of time, W = Pt. The SI unit is the joule (watt-second); the commercial unit is the kilowatt-hour (kWh), also called the Board of Trade unit or simply one 'unit' — the energy used by a 1 kW load running for 1 hour. 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Electricity bills are in kWh: a 2 kW heater run for 3 hours uses 2 × 3 = 6 kWh = 2.16 × 10⁷ J.

concepts.plainText: W = P × t = V × I × t = I² × R × t = (V² / R) × t

concepts.text: Ideal and Practical Sources
Source models used in circuit analysis:
items: Ideal voltage source: terminal voltage stays fixed whatever current is drawn; internal resistance R_int = 0.
Practical voltage source: an EMF E in series with a small internal resistance r; terminal voltage V = E − Ir falls as load current rises, and the short-circuit current is E/r.
Ideal current source: delivers a fixed current whatever the load voltage; internal resistance R_int = ∞ (in parallel).
Practical current source: an ideal current source in parallel with a large but finite resistance.
To 'kill' a source in superposition or Thevenin analysis, replace a voltage source by a short circuit and a current source by an open circuit.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Charge, Power and Energy

Current can be linked to the motion of the individual charge carriers. Suppose a conductor of area A contains n free electrons per cubic metre, each drifting with an average velocity v. In a time t every electron within a length vt of the wire, that is nAvt electrons, crosses a given section, carrying a charge nAvte. Dividing by t gives the current, I = nAev. For copper n ≈ 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, so 2 A in a 2.5 mm² wire corresponds to a drift speed of only about 0.06 mm/s.

concepts.latex: I = n A e v_d, \qquad Q = It, \qquad N = \frac{Q}{e}
concepts.plainText: I = n A e v_d ; Q = I t ; number of electrons N = Q/e

concepts.text: The drift speed is tiny, yet a lamp lights the instant the switch is closed. This is because the conductor is already full of free electrons: closing the switch sets up the electric field along the whole circuit almost at the speed of light, and every electron everywhere starts drifting at once. Energy is carried by the field, not by electrons travelling from the source to the load.

When a practical source of EMF E and internal resistance r feeds a load R, the current is I = E/(R + r) and the terminal voltage is V = ER/(R + r). The source generates power EI, of which I²R reaches the load and I²r is wasted as heat inside the source. The fraction delivered, V/E = R/(R + r), is the efficiency of the source; it approaches 100% when R is much larger than r. When a battery is being charged, current is forced into its positive terminal and the charger must supply V = E + Ir.

concepts.plainText: I = E/(R + r); efficiency η = I²R/(EI) = V/E = R/(R + r)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - battery feeding a load
E = 12 V, r = 0.4 ohm, load R = 5.6 ohm
Step 1: I = E / (R + r) = 12 / 6.0 = 2 A
Step 2: terminal voltage V = E - I r = 12 - 2 x 0.4 = 11.2 V
Step 3: power generated = E I = 12 x 2 = 24 W
Step 4: power to load = I^2 R = 4 x 5.6 = 22.4 W; loss inside = I^2 r = 1.6 W
Step 5: efficiency = 22.4 / 24 = 93.3 %  (= R / (R + r) = 5.6 / 6)

Worked example 2 - heating water and the cost of energy
10 kg of water is heated from 15 C to 65 C by a 2 kW, 230 V heater, efficiency 90 %.
c(water) = 4200 J/(kg C), tariff Rs 10 per kWh
Step 1: heat needed = m c dT = 10 x 4200 x 50 = 2.1 MJ
Step 2: electrical input = 2.1 MJ / 0.9 = 2.333 MJ
Step 3: in kWh: 2.333e6 / 3.6e6 = 0.648 kWh
Step 4: time = energy / power = 2.333e6 / 2000 = 1167 s = 19.4 min
Step 5: cost = 0.648 x 10 = Rs 6.48; current = 2000 / 230 = 8.70 A

Circuit analysis uses the passive sign convention to decide whether an element absorbs or delivers power. If the current enters the terminal marked + and the product VI is positive, the element absorbs power (a resistor, or a battery being charged). If the current enters the − terminal, the element delivers power VI to the rest of the circuit, as a battery does when it discharges. In any complete circuit the power delivered by the sources equals the total power absorbed.

concepts.text: Common mistakes in power and energy problems:
items: Multiplying kW by minutes or seconds and calling the answer kWh; convert the time to hours first.
Using P = V²/R with a resistance found at a different voltage for a non-ohmic lamp; the resistance of a rated lamp is assumed constant only when the question says so.
Adding the ratings of lamps connected in series; for equal-voltage lamps in series the total power is less than that of either lamp alone.
Forgetting efficiency: output power = efficiency × input power, so the input (and the bill) is output ÷ efficiency.
Treating mAh as energy; mAh is charge, and energy in Wh = voltage × Ah.

In parallel with the element, and ideally have zero resistance
In series with the element, and ideally have infinite resistance

options: From the negative terminal to the positive terminal, with the electron flow
From the positive terminal to the negative terminal, with the electron flow
From the positive terminal to the negative terminal, opposite to electron flow
questions.explanation: Conventional current is the direction positive charge would move: from + to − outside the source. Electrons actually move from − to +.

questions.explanation: V = E − Ir, so V = E only when I = 0 (open circuit). On short circuit the terminal voltage falls to zero.

The energy gained by one electron moving through a potential difference of 1 V, about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
The potential difference needed to move one electron, 1 V
The power used by one electron in 1 second

questions.questionText: Electrons drift through a wire at well under a millimetre per second, yet a lamp several metres away lights almost as soon as the switch is closed. This is because:
options: Electrons leave the battery at nearly the speed of light
The lamp stores charge and releases it when the switch closes
The current flows only on the surface of the wire
The electric field is set up along the whole circuit almost instantly, so free electrons everywhere start drifting together
questions.explanation: The wire is already full of free electrons. Closing the switch establishes the field throughout the circuit at close to the speed of light, and all the electrons begin to drift at once.

questions.explanation: The drop inside is 6.0 − 5.4 = 0.6 V, so r = 0.6/3 = 0.2 Ω. (1.8 Ω is the load resistance 5.4/3.)

questions.explanation: While charging, current is forced into the positive terminal against the EMF, so V = E + Ir = 12 + 10 × 0.1 = 13 V.

questions.explanation: P = I²R = 3² × 8 = 72 W.

questions.explanation: P = V²/R, so V_max = √(PR) = √(0.25 × 1000) ≈ 15.8 V (the corresponding current is 15.8 mA). Multiplying P × R gives 250 V, and √P alone gives 0.5 V.

questions.questionText: Two heaters are rated for the same voltage, one at 500 W and the other at 1000 W. Compared with the 500 W heater, the 1000 W heater has:
questions.explanation: R = V²/P, so at equal rated voltage the resistance is inversely proportional to the power rating: doubling P halves R.

questions.explanation: Time = capacity/current = 3000 mAh / 250 mA = 12 h.

questions.explanation: Current entering the − terminal means the element pushes charge up to the higher potential, so it acts as a source: it delivers P = VI = 5 × 2 = 10 W.

questions.questionText: Which statement about EMF and potential difference is correct?

EMF and potential difference are both zero when the circuit is open
The terminal potential difference of a cell on load is always greater than its EMF
EMF is measured in joules and potential difference in volts

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a unit of energy?
questions.explanation: The kilowatt is a unit of power. A watt-second is a joule, and the electron-volt and kilowatt-hour are also energy units.

questions.questionText: An ideal current source has:

Infinite internal resistance, and its current is set by the load
Infinite internal resistance, and its terminal voltage is set by the load
Zero internal resistance and a fixed terminal voltage

subtopics.title: Conducting & Insulating Materials
subtopics.subtitle: Conductors, semiconductors and insulators: free electrons, resistivity, band gap, uses

concepts.text: Classification by Conductivity

Every material is classed as a conductor, a semiconductor or an insulator according to how easily it lets current flow. Conductors (metals) have a large number of free electrons — roughly one per atom, about 10²⁸ per m³ — so their resistivity is very low, 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ω·m, and they allow easy flow of current. Insulators have almost no free electrons because their valence electrons are tightly bound; their resistivity is enormous, above about 10¹⁰ Ω·m, and they block the flow of current. Semiconductors such as silicon and germanium lie between the two (roughly 10⁻⁵ to 10⁶ Ω·m), and their conductivity can be controlled by doping, temperature and light.

rows: Rubber, glass, plastic, wood, mica, air

concepts.text: Energy-Band View

In the band theory of solids the electrons occupy a valence band and a higher conduction band separated by a forbidden gap E_g. In a conductor the two bands overlap (or the conduction band is partly filled), so electrons move freely under even a small electric field. In a semiconductor the gap is small — about 1.1 eV for silicon and 0.7 eV for germanium — so thermal energy at room temperature lifts some electrons across it and creates electron-hole pairs; more heat or doping increases the carrier count. In an insulator the gap exceeds about 3 eV (5.5 eV for diamond), and practically no electron can cross it at ordinary temperatures and voltages.
Common Conducting Materials

Silver is the best conductor of all but is too costly for general use, so it is reserved for contacts and plating. Copper is the standard wiring material because it combines low resistivity with ductility, strength and easy soldering. Aluminium has about 1.6 times the resistivity of copper but only 30% of its density, which makes it lighter and cheaper for a given resistance — the reason overhead transmission lines use aluminium conductors with a steel core (ACSR). Tungsten has a high resistivity and the highest melting point of any metal (about 3400 °C), which suits lamp filaments. Alloys such as nichrome, manganin and constantan have high resistivity and serve as heater elements and precision resistors. The conductivity order to remember is silver > copper > gold > aluminium.
Insulating Materials and Dielectric Strength

Insulators confine current to its intended path and protect people from shock: rubber, PVC and polyethylene sheath cables; porcelain and glass support overhead lines; mica separates heater elements and commutator segments; paper, transformer oil and varnish insulate windings; dry air and SF₆ gas insulate switchgear. Dielectric strength is the maximum electric field an insulator can withstand without breaking down, quoted in kV/mm (or V/m); when it is exceeded the material punctures and conducts, and the breakdown voltage of a sheet is V_b = E_b × thickness. A good insulator also needs very high resistivity, low dielectric loss, good mechanical strength and resistance to heat and moisture.
Effect of Temperature

Heating a metal makes its lattice ions vibrate more strongly and scatter the free electrons, so its resistivity rises — a positive temperature coefficient (α ≈ +0.004/°C for copper). Heating a semiconductor or an insulator instead frees more charge carriers across the band gap, so their resistivity falls sharply — a negative temperature coefficient. This is why an NTC thermistor is made from semiconductor material and why the insulation resistance of a cable drops on a hot day. Alloys such as manganin and constantan have almost zero coefficient, making them ideal for standard resistors and meter shunts; carbon also has a small negative coefficient.
Choosing a material:
items: Conductor: lowest resistivity and cost, ductility, mechanical strength, corrosion resistance — copper for general wiring, aluminium for overhead lines, silver plating for contacts.

High-resistance element: high resistivity, high melting point, low temperature coefficient, oxidation resistance — nichrome for heaters, manganin or constantan for precision resistors, tungsten for filaments.

Insulator: very high resistivity, high dielectric strength, low loss, thermal and mechanical robustness — PVC or rubber for cables, porcelain or glass for line insulators, mica for heaters and commutators, oil and paper for transformers.
Semiconductor: controllable conductivity — silicon for diodes, transistors, ICs and solar cells; germanium in early devices; gallium arsenide for high-frequency and optoelectronic devices.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Conductors and Insulators

A free electron in a metal is accelerated by the applied field and then scattered by vibrating lattice ions and by impurity atoms, so it gains only a small average drift velocity, typically a fraction of a millimetre per second. The conductivity follows as σ = neμ, where the mobility μ = eτ/m is set by the mean time τ between collisions. Heating the metal shortens τ, so its resistivity rises almost linearly with temperature. Impurity and alloying atoms shorten τ further; the lattice and impurity parts of resistivity simply add (Matthiessen's rule), which is why alloys have much higher resistivity and a much smaller temperature coefficient than the pure metals they are made from.

concepts.plainText: v_d = I / (n e A) ;  σ = n e² τ / m = n e μ

concepts.text: The value of the temperature coefficient depends on the reference temperature at which the resistance is measured. If α₀ is referred to 0 °C, the coefficient referred to t °C is α_t = α₀/(1 + α₀t), which is smaller: copper has α₀ ≈ 0.00427 per °C but α₂₀ ≈ 0.00393 per °C. When a resistance is known at t₁ and wanted at t₂, take the ratio of the two (1 + α₀t) factors instead of simply adding α₀(t₂ − t₁) to R₁; that shortcut is exact only when α is referred to t₁ itself.

Worked example 1 - copper wire resistance and its rise with temperature
Given: l = 500 m, A = 2.5 mm² = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m², ρ = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m at 20 °C, α₂₀ = 0.00393 per °C
R₂₀ = ρl/A = (1.72 × 10⁻⁸ × 500)/(2.5 × 10⁻⁶) = 3.44 Ω
At 60 °C: R₆₀ = R₂₀[1 + α₂₀(60 − 20)] = 3.44 × (1 + 0.1572) = 3.98 Ω
Rise = 0.54 Ω, about 15.7 % for a 40 °C rise

Worked example 2 - aluminium instead of copper, same length and resistance
ρ_Cu = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, ρ_Al = 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m; density Cu = 8.9 g/cm³, Al = 2.7 g/cm³
Same R and l, so A is proportional to ρ: A_Al/A_Cu = 2.8/1.7 = 1.65
Mass is proportional to density × A: m_Al/m_Cu = 1.65 × 2.7/8.9 = 0.50
Result: the aluminium conductor weighs about half as much for the same resistance,
although its diameter is √1.65 = 1.28 times larger

Insulation resistance is measured radially, from the conductor out through the insulation to the sheath, so the current path is short and its area is very large, the opposite of conductor resistance. For a single-core cable of length l, conductor radius r₁ and insulation outer radius r₂, adding up thin cylindrical shells gives R_ins = (ρ/2πl) ln(r₂/r₁). A longer cable therefore has more leakage paths in parallel and a lower insulation resistance, whereas its conductor resistance is higher.

concepts.plainText: R_ins = (ρ / 2π l) × ln(r2 / r1)

concepts.text: Common mistakes and special cases:
items: Leaving the area in mm² in R = ρl/A: 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², and forgetting this makes R a million times too small.
Adding α₀(t₂ − t₁) to R₁ when α is referred to 0 °C; use the ratio of the (1 + α₀t) factors instead.
Stretching a wire keeps its volume constant: if the length becomes k times, the area becomes 1/k and R becomes k² times.
Confusing dielectric strength (kV/mm, a material property) with breakdown voltage (kV, which also depends on thickness).
Carbon, electrolytes and semiconductors have negative temperature coefficients; a tungsten lamp's cold resistance is only about a tenth of its hot value, hence the switch-on surge.
Some metals and compounds become superconductors below a critical temperature and lose all resistance; mercury, at about 4.2 K, was the first found.
A pure semiconductor at 0 K has an empty conduction band and behaves as an insulator.

concepts.text: Insulation resistance falls as cable length increases (R_ins is proportional to 1/l), while conductor resistance rises with length (R is proportional to l). Insulation resistance also drops sharply when the insulation is hot or damp, so readings must be compared at the same temperature.

formulas.plainText: ρ = R A / l ;  σ = 1 / ρ

notes.text: Conductivity order to memorise: silver > copper > gold > aluminium (> tungsten). Copper is used instead of silver because of cost; aluminium beats copper for overhead lines because of weight and cost, not conductivity.

Sign of the temperature coefficient: metals positive, semiconductors and insulators negative. A question saying 'resistance decreases on heating' points to a semiconductor, carbon or an electrolyte — never to a pure metal.
Dielectric strength (kV/mm) is a property of the insulating material; the breakdown voltage (kV) of a part also depends on its thickness: V_b = E_b × d.

Material-to-property pairs that recur in exams: manganin and constantan — near-zero temperature coefficient (standard resistors, shunts); nichrome — high resistivity plus high working temperature (heaters); tungsten — highest melting point (filaments); mica — heat-resistant insulator with very high dielectric strength.

flashcards.front: Why is aluminium used for overhead transmission lines even though copper conducts better?
flashcards.back: Aluminium has about 1.6 times copper's resistivity but only 30% of its density, so for the same resistance the line is lighter and cheaper; it is reinforced with a steel core (ACSR) for strength.

flashcards.front: What are the approximate band gaps of silicon, germanium and a typical insulator?
flashcards.back: Silicon ≈ 1.1 eV, germanium ≈ 0.7 eV; insulators have gaps above about 3 eV, while conductors have overlapping bands (no gap).

flashcards.front: Which metal is used for lamp filaments, and why?
flashcards.back: Tungsten, because it has the highest melting point of any metal (about 3400 °C) together with a fairly high resistivity.

flashcards.front: What does dielectric strength measure, and what is its value for air?
flashcards.back: The maximum electric field an insulator can withstand before breakdown, in kV/mm; air is about 3 kV/mm.

questions.questionText: The resistivity of a good conductor such as copper at room temperature is of the order of:
questions.explanation: Copper has ρ ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m; conductors lie in the 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ω·m range, semiconductors around 10⁻⁵ to 10⁶ Ω·m and insulators above 10¹⁰ Ω·m.

questions.questionText: The temperature coefficient of resistance of a semiconductor such as silicon is:
questions.explanation: Heating a semiconductor frees more electron-hole pairs across the band gap, so its resistance falls with temperature (negative coefficient); pure metals have a positive coefficient.

questions.questionText: Nichrome is preferred over copper for the heating element of an electric heater mainly because nichrome has:
options: High resistivity and a high working temperature
questions.explanation: A heater needs a large resistance in a short length (P = I²R) that survives red heat without oxidising; nichrome's resistivity is about 60 times that of copper and it withstands about 1000 °C, whereas copper would need an impractically long wire and would oxidise.

questions.questionText: A copper wire 200 m long has a cross-sectional area of 2 mm². Taking ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, its resistance is:
The forbidden energy gap of diamond, a typical insulator, is about:
questions.explanation: Insulators have band gaps above about 3 eV; diamond's is about 5.5 eV, while germanium is about 0.7 eV, silicon about 1.1 eV and conductors have no gap.

questions.questionText: The resistivity of annealed copper is 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m. Its conductivity is:
In a metallic conductor, the valence band and the conduction band:
options: Are separated by a gap of about 1 eV
Overlap, so there is no forbidden gap
Are separated by a gap of more than 3 eV
questions.explanation: In metals the bands overlap (or the conduction band is partly filled), so electrons move freely under a small field; a gap of about 1 eV marks a semiconductor and more than 3 eV an insulator.

questions.questionText: A wire sample 2 m long with a cross-sectional area of 0.5 mm² has a resistance of 0.112 Ω at 20 °C. The material is most likely:
questions.explanation: ρ = RA/l = 0.112 × 0.5 × 10⁻⁶/2 = 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, which matches aluminium (silver 1.6, copper 1.7, nichrome about 110, all × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m).

questions.questionText: The filament of an incandescent lamp is made of:
questions.explanation: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal (about 3400 °C) and a fairly high resistivity, so it can run white-hot.

questions.questionText: A copper coil has a resistance of 10 Ω at 0 °C. Taking α₀ = 0.00427 per °C, its resistance at 50 °C is:
Manganin is used for standard resistors and ammeter shunts mainly because it has:
options: The lowest resistivity of all alloys
A negative temperature coefficient of resistance
An almost zero temperature coefficient of resistance
questions.explanation: Manganin's temperature coefficient is about 0.00001 per °C, so its resistance hardly changes as it warms; that stability, not low resistivity, is what standards and shunts need.

questions.questionText: A copper field winding measures 50 Ω at 20 °C and 58 Ω after a long run. Taking α₂₀ = 0.00393 per °C, the average winding temperature is about:
Which of the following is an insulator?
questions.explanation: Mica is an insulator with very high dielectric strength; graphite and aluminium conduct, and germanium is a semiconductor.

questions.questionText: The temperature coefficient of resistance of a metal referred to 0 °C is 0.004 per °C. Its temperature coefficient referred to 50 °C is:
questions.explanation: α₅₀ = α₀/(1 + α₀ × 50) = 0.004/(1 + 0.2) = 0.00333 per °C; the coefficient is smaller when referred to a higher temperature.

questions.questionText: In an ACSR overhead conductor, the steel core is provided mainly to:
options: Reduce the resistance of the conductor
Give the tensile strength needed for long spans
Insulate the conductor from the tower
Raise the conductivity at high temperature
questions.explanation: The aluminium strands carry the current; the galvanised steel core gives the mechanical (tensile) strength that aluminium alone lacks, allowing longer spans with less sag.

questions.questionText: A coil has a resistance of 40 Ω at 20 °C. Taking α₀ = 0.004 per °C (referred to 0 °C), its resistance at 70 °C is:
Which statement about the temperature coefficient of resistance of materials is NOT correct?
options: Pure metals have a positive temperature coefficient of resistance
Semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance
Insulators have a positive temperature coefficient of resistance
Manganin has a nearly zero temperature coefficient of resistance
questions.explanation: Heating an insulator frees more charge carriers, so its resistance falls: insulators have a negative temperature coefficient. The other three statements are true.

questions.questionText: A mica sheet 0.2 mm thick has a dielectric strength of 60 kV/mm. The voltage at which it breaks down is:
questions.explanation: V_b = E_b × d = 60 kV/mm × 0.2 mm = 12 kV.

questions.questionText: Dielectric strength of an insulating material is commonly expressed in:
questions.explanation: Dielectric strength is the maximum electric field the material withstands before breakdown, i.e. voltage per unit thickness, such as kV/mm (Ω·m is resistivity).

questions.questionText: A cable for 33 kV is insulated with a material of dielectric strength 12 kV/mm. For a factor of safety of 2, the minimum insulation thickness is:
questions.explanation: Design withstand voltage = 2 × 33 = 66 kV, so d = V/E_b = 66/12 = 5.5 mm; ignoring the factor of safety gives 2.75 mm.

questions.questionText: Which list is in DECREASING order of electrical conductivity?
questions.explanation: Resistivities at 20 °C are about 1.6, 1.7, 2.4 and 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m for silver, copper, gold and aluminium, so conductivity falls in that order.

questions.questionText: Two parallel plates 2 cm apart are separated by dry air of dielectric strength 30 kV/cm. The maximum voltage that can be applied before the air breaks down is:
questions.explanation: V_b = E_b × d = 30 kV/cm × 2 cm = 60 kV (30 kV/cm is the same as 3 kV/mm).

questions.questionText: The resistance of a pure metal rises with temperature mainly because:
options: The number of free electrons decreases
The lattice ions vibrate more and scatter the free electrons more often
The band gap of the metal widens
The cross-sectional area of the conductor shrinks
questions.explanation: The number of free electrons in a metal is essentially fixed; heating increases lattice vibration, which shortens the time between collisions and lowers the mobility, so resistivity rises.

questions.questionText: Copper has about 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³ and an electron mobility of 4.3 × 10⁻³ m²/V·s. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, its resistivity is about:
Below its critical temperature, a superconducting material:
options: Has a resistance that rises sharply
questions.explanation: Superconductivity is the complete disappearance of DC resistance below a critical temperature (for mercury about 4.2 K); current can then circulate without loss.

questions.questionText: Intrinsic silicon at 300 K has n_i = 1.5 × 10¹⁶ per m³, μ_n = 0.135 m²/V·s and μ_p = 0.048 m²/V·s. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, its resistivity is about:
questions.explanation: σ = n_i e(μ_n + μ_p) = 1.5 × 10¹⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.183 = 4.39 × 10⁻⁴ S/m, so ρ = 1/σ = 2.28 × 10³ Ω·m. Using only the electron mobility gives 3.09 × 10³ Ω·m.

questions.questionText: SF₆ gas is used in high-voltage circuit breakers because it:
options: Is a good conductor that bypasses the arc
Is lighter than air and disperses quickly
Has a high dielectric strength and, being electronegative, quenches arcs well
questions.explanation: SF₆ is a heavy, non-flammable, electronegative gas that captures free electrons; its dielectric strength is about 2 to 3 times that of air, so it both insulates and quenches arcs.

questions.questionText: A wire is drawn out so that its diameter becomes half the original value, its volume remaining the same. Its resistance becomes:
questions.explanation: Halving the diameter makes the area 1/4; constant volume makes the length 4 times, so R = ρl/A becomes 4 × 4 = 16 times.

questions.questionText: In a power transformer, the transformer oil serves to:
options: Insulate the windings and carry heat away from them
questions.explanation: Transformer oil is a liquid insulator with a dielectric strength of about 10 to 15 kV/mm, and it circulates to transfer heat from windings and core to the tank and radiators.

questions.questionText: Wire A has length 2l and diameter d; wire B, of the same material, has length l and diameter 2d. The ratio R_A : R_B is:
questions.explanation: R is proportional to l/d²: R_A/R_B = (2l/d²)/(l/4d²) = 8, so R_A : R_B = 8 : 1.

questions.questionText: Absorption of moisture by an insulating material:
options: Lowers its insulation resistance and its dielectric strength
Has no effect on its electrical properties
Gives it a positive temperature coefficient
questions.explanation: Water, with dissolved impurities, provides conducting paths through and over the insulation, so both its resistance and its breakdown strength fall; this is why insulation is dried and sealed.

questions.questionText: For the same length and the same resistance, the ratio of the mass of an aluminium conductor to that of a copper conductor is about (ρ_Al = 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, ρ_Cu = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, densities 2.7 and 8.9 g/cm³):
questions.explanation: Same R and l need A_Al/A_Cu = 2.8/1.7 = 1.65; mass ratio = 1.65 × 2.7/8.9 = 0.50, so aluminium is about half the weight (0.30 is the density ratio alone).

questions.questionText: In an intrinsic semiconductor at room temperature, electron-hole pairs are produced mainly by:
options: The magnetic field of the current
questions.explanation: At room temperature some valence electrons gain enough thermal energy to cross the band gap, each leaving a hole behind; doping adds carriers of one type and does not make an intrinsic semiconductor.

questions.questionText: A copper conductor of cross-section 50 mm² is to be replaced by an aluminium conductor of the same length and resistance. Taking ρ_Cu = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m and ρ_Al = 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, the aluminium cross-section needed is about:
questions.explanation: For equal R and l, A is proportional to ρ: A_Al = 50 × 2.8/1.7 = 82.4 mm². Inverting the ratio gives the wrong 30.4 mm².

questions.questionText: Under the standard thermal classification of insulating materials, the maximum permissible temperature for Class B insulation is:
questions.explanation: The classes are Y 90 °C, A 105 °C, E 120 °C, B 130 °C, F 155 °C, H 180 °C and C above 180 °C.

questions.questionText: A single-core cable 2 km long has a conductor radius of 5 mm and an insulation outer radius of 12.5 mm. The insulation resistivity is 5 × 10¹² Ω·m. Its insulation resistance is about:
questions.explanation: R_ins = (ρ/2πl) ln(r₂/r₁) = (5 × 10¹²/(2π × 2000)) × ln 2.5 = 3.98 × 10⁸ × 0.916 = 3.65 × 10⁸ Ω, about 365 MΩ. Using log₁₀ gives 158 MΩ; leaving out 2π gives 2290 MΩ.

questions.questionText: Compared with the pure metals it is made from, an alloy such as nichrome generally has:
options: Higher resistivity and a lower temperature coefficient
Lower resistivity and a higher temperature coefficient
The same resistivity but a zero temperature coefficient
Lower resistivity and a negative temperature coefficient
questions.explanation: Alloying atoms scatter electrons and add a large, nearly temperature-independent part to the resistivity, so ρ rises and the fractional change with temperature (α) falls.

questions.questionText: The insulation resistance of a cable is 500 MΩ for a 1 km length. The insulation resistance of 2.5 km of the same cable is:
questions.explanation: Insulation resistance is inversely proportional to length (more leakage paths in parallel): 500/2.5 = 200 MΩ.

questions.questionText: Silicon is preferred to germanium for most semiconductor devices mainly because silicon:
options: Has a smaller band gap, so it conducts more easily
Has a larger band gap, so its leakage current is smaller and it can work at higher temperatures
Has more free electrons at room temperature
Is a better conductor than germanium
questions.explanation: Silicon's band gap (about 1.1 eV) exceeds germanium's (about 0.7 eV), so far fewer carriers are thermally generated; its reverse leakage is much smaller and it can operate up to about 150 °C to 200 °C.

questions.questionText: A 1 kW, 230 V heater element is to be wound from nichrome wire of cross-section 0.2 mm² and resistivity 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m. The length of wire needed is about:
Fuse elements for small current ratings are commonly made of:
questions.explanation: A fuse element needs a low melting point so it melts quickly on overcurrent; tin-lead alloy suits small ratings, whereas tungsten and nichrome are chosen precisely because they survive high temperatures.

questions.questionText: Three materials at room temperature have resistivities A = 2.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, B = 0.5 Ω·m and C = 10¹³ Ω·m. They should be classified respectively as:
questions.explanation: Conductors have resistivities of roughly 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ω·m (A is aluminium), semiconductors lie in the broad middle range (B is close to intrinsic germanium), and insulators exceed about 10⁸ Ω·m (C is typical of glass or mica).

questions.questionText: Which of the following materials has a negative temperature coefficient of resistance?
questions.explanation: Carbon's resistance falls as it gets hotter (negative coefficient); copper, aluminium and tungsten are pure metals with positive coefficients.

questions.questionText: A copper coil (α = +0.004 per °C) is connected in series with a carbon resistor (α = −0.0005 per °C) so that the total resistance of 100 Ω does not change with temperature. The two resistances are:
questions.explanation: For zero change, R_Cu × 0.004 = R_C × 0.0005, so R_C = 8R_Cu; with R_Cu + R_C = 100 Ω, R_Cu = 100/9 = 11.1 Ω and R_C = 88.9 Ω.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a desirable property of a good insulating material?
questions.explanation: A good insulator should have low dielectric loss so it does not heat up under AC stress; high dielectric strength, high resistance and low moisture absorption are all desirable.

questions.questionText: A manganin shunt with α = 0.00001 per °C warms up by 50 °C. The percentage change in its resistance is about:
questions.explanation: ΔR/R = αΔt = 0.00001 × 50 = 0.0005 = 0.05 %; a copper shunt (α ≈ 0.0039) would change by about 19.5 %.

questions.questionText: Copper rather than silver is used for general wiring mainly because:
options: Copper has a lower resistivity than silver
Silver is far more costly, while copper's conductivity is only slightly lower
Silver cannot be drawn into wires
Copper has a negative temperature coefficient of resistance
questions.explanation: Silver (1.6 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m) conducts slightly better than copper (1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m), but its cost rules it out for bulk wiring; copper is ductile, strong, easily soldered and much cheaper.

questions.questionText: An 11 kV cable has insulation 3 mm thick made of a material with dielectric strength 20 kV/mm. The factor of safety of the insulation is about:
questions.explanation: Breakdown voltage = 20 × 3 = 60 kV; factor of safety = 60/11 = 5.45.

questions.questionText: The insulators that support overhead line conductors on poles and towers are usually made of:
questions.explanation: Porcelain and toughened glass combine good dielectric strength with high mechanical strength and resistance to weather, which outdoor line insulators need.

subtopics.title: Series & Parallel Circuits
subtopics.subtitle: Rules for R, V and I; voltage and current dividers; series-parallel reduction; cells

concepts.text: Series and Parallel Combinations
Series Circuit

In a series circuit the elements are connected end to end so that there is only one path for the current. The same current flows through every element, the applied voltage divides among them in proportion to their resistances, and the total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances — always larger than the largest single resistance. If one element fails open, the whole circuit is broken; this is why a string of series-wired decorative lamps all go out when one bulb fails.
Series rules:
items: Current: the same through all — I = I₁ = I₂ = I₃
Voltage: divides — V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃, each drop being IR
Resistance: adds — R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃; for n equal resistors R_total = nR
Power: adds — P = P₁ + P₂ + P₃; the largest resistance dissipates the most power (P = I²R)
Key point: if one component fails (opens), the entire circuit stops.

concepts.text: Parallel Circuit

In a parallel circuit all elements are connected between the same two nodes, so each has the same voltage across it and the total current divides among the branches — the smallest resistance carries the largest current. The reciprocal of the total resistance is the sum of the reciprocals (conductances add), so the equivalent resistance is always smaller than the smallest branch. If one branch fails the others keep working, which is why household appliances are wired in parallel across the 230 V supply and can be switched independently.
Parallel rules:
items: Voltage: the same across all — V = V₁ = V₂ = V₃
Current: divides — I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃, each branch current being V/R
Resistance: 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃, i.e. G_total = G₁ + G₂ + G₃
n equal resistors: R_total = R/n; two resistors: product over sum
Key point: if one component fails, the others still work.

concepts.text: For two resistors in parallel use the product-over-sum shortcut: Rp = R1R2 / (R1 + R2). It applies to two resistors at a time only — for three, combine two first and then repeat.
Voltage Divider, Current Divider and Reduction

Two resistors in series form a voltage divider: the supply voltage splits in the ratio of the resistances, V₁ = V × R₁/(R₁ + R₂). Two resistors in parallel form a current divider: the total current splits in the inverse ratio of the resistances, I₁ = I × R₂/(R₁ + R₂) — a branch current is proportional to the other branch's resistance, or equivalently to its own conductance. These two results give voltages and currents directly without first solving for the whole circuit.

concepts.latex: V_1 = V\frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2}, \qquad I_1 = I\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}

concepts.text: Series-parallel reduction method:
items: Identify groups that are purely series (same current, no junction between them) or purely parallel (connected between the same two nodes).
Replace each group by its equivalent: add series resistances; use product-over-sum or reciprocals for parallel ones.
Redraw the simplified circuit and repeat until a single resistance remains, then find the total current I = V/R_eq.
Work back outwards, using the divider rules to find each branch current and voltage drop.
Check: the drops along any series path add up to the supply voltage, and the branch currents at a node add up to the current entering it.

concepts.text: Cells in series and parallel (EMF E, internal resistance r each):
items: n cells in series: total EMF = nE, total internal resistance = nr — used to obtain a higher voltage.
n identical cells in parallel: EMF = E, internal resistance = r/n — used to obtain a larger current or capacity (Ah).
Never connect cells of different EMF in parallel: the higher one drives a circulating current through the lower.
Terminal voltage of any battery on load: V = E − Ir.

concepts.text: Worked example: a 6 Ω resistor is in parallel with a 3 Ω resistor, and the pair is in series with a 4 Ω resistor across a 12 V supply. Parallel pair: R_p = (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 2 Ω. Total: R_eq = 2 + 4 = 6 Ω, so I = 12/6 = 2 A. Voltage across the pair = 2 × 2 = 4 V and across the 4 Ω resistor = 2 × 4 = 8 V (check: 4 + 8 = 12 V). Branch currents: 4/6 = 0.67 A through the 6 Ω and 4/3 = 1.33 A through the 3 Ω (check: they add to 2 A, and the smaller resistor carries the larger current).
Going Deeper: Series-Parallel Networks

Both combination rules come straight from Kirchhoff's laws. In series the single current I flows through every resistor, so KVL gives V = IR₁ + IR₂ + … = I(R₁ + R₂ + …), and the bracket is the series total. In parallel the common voltage V drives V/R₁, V/R₂, … through the branches, and KCL gives I = V(1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …), so the conductances add. Each extra series resistor adds another drop, and each extra parallel branch adds another path, which is why a series total always exceeds its largest member and a parallel equivalent always lies below its smallest.

concepts.plainText: Three in parallel: Rp = R1 R2 R3 / (R1 R2 + R2 R3 + R3 R1)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - ladder network, reduce from the far end
30 V supply -> 5 Ω in series -> node A; 20 Ω from A to the return line;
also from A: 6 Ω in series with 14 Ω to the return line
Far branch: 6 + 14 = 20 Ω
At A: 20 Ω || 20 Ω = 10 Ω
Total: R_eq = 5 + 10 = 15 Ω, so I = 30/15 = 2 A
V_A = 2 × 10 = 20 V; current in the 20 Ω shunt = 20/20 = 1 A; far branch = 1 A
V(14 Ω) = 14 V and V(6 Ω) = 6 V (check: 6 + 14 = 20 V = V_A)

Worked example 2 - a voltage divider under load
Unloaded: 12 V across R1 = 4 kΩ (top) and R2 = 2 kΩ (bottom)
V_out = 12 × 2/(4 + 2) = 4 V
Load R_L = 2 kΩ across R2: R2 || R_L = 1 kΩ
V_out = 12 × 1/(4 + 1) = 2.4 V (a 40 % fall)
Load R_L = 200 kΩ: R2 || R_L = 1.980 kΩ, V_out = 12 × 1.980/5.980 = 3.97 V
Rule: keep R_L at least 10 times, preferably 100 times, the lower divider resistor

Worked example 3 - lamps of different rating in series (resistance taken as constant)
Two 230 V lamps, 60 W and 100 W, in series across 230 V
R60 = 230²/60 = 881.7 Ω; R100 = 230²/100 = 529 Ω
I = 230/(881.7 + 529) = 0.163 A
P60 = 0.163² × 881.7 = 23.4 W; P100 = 0.163² × 529 = 14.1 W
In series the 60 W lamp glows brighter (same I, higher R);
in parallel across 230 V the 100 W lamp is brighter (same V, lower R)

rows: Divides; smallest R takes the most
Conductances add; less than the smallest

concepts.text: When N identical cells are arranged in m parallel rows, each row having n cells in series (N = mn), the battery has EMF nE and internal resistance nr/m. The current in an external resistor R is nE/(R + nr/m), and for a fixed number of cells it is greatest when the arrangement makes the internal resistance equal to the external resistance, R = nr/m, which is the maximum power transfer condition in another form.

concepts.plainText: I = nE / (R + nr/m) ;  maximum when R = nr/m

concepts.text: Special cases shorten many problems. A resistor with a short circuit across it carries no current and can be deleted, and so can a resistor that leads only to an open end. In a balanced Wheatstone bridge (R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄) the two midpoints are at the same potential, so the element bridging them carries no current and may be removed or shorted without changing anything. A uniform wire of resistance R cut into n equal pieces that are then joined in parallel gives R/n².
Common mistakes:
items: Using product-over-sum on three resistors at once; it is valid for exactly two.
Swapping resistances in the current-divider rule: the current in R₁ is I × R₂/(R₁ + R₂).
Ignoring the load on a voltage divider: a load across the lower resistor always lowers the output.
Treating two resistors as series when a branch leaves the node between them; series requires the same current with no junction in between.
Assuming the higher-wattage lamp is always brighter: true in parallel, but in series the lower-wattage (higher-resistance) lamp dissipates more.
Forgetting internal resistance: n cells in series have nr, n identical cells in parallel have r/n.

concepts.text: For power questions, pick the formula that holds the common quantity fixed: in series the current is common, so use P = I²R and the largest resistor dissipates most; in parallel the voltage is common, so use P = V²/R and the smallest resistor dissipates most.

formulas.latex: R_s = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots + R_n \quad (n \text{ equal: } nR)
formulas.plainText: Rs = R1 + R2 + ... + Rn  (n equal: nR)

formulas.latex: E_s = nE,\; r_s = nr \qquad E_p = E,\; r_p = \frac{r}{n}
formulas.plainText: Series cells: E_s = nE, r_s = nr ;  parallel cells: E_p = E, r_p = r/n

notes.text: A parallel equivalent is always less than the smallest branch; a series total is always more than the largest member. Use this to strike out impossible options before calculating.
Product-over-sum works for TWO resistors only. For three or more, use reciprocals or apply the shortcut twice (combine a pair, then combine the result with the third).

Two equal resistors R in parallel give R/2, three give R/3, n give R/n. In series, n equal resistors give nR — so n equal resistors in series have n² times the resistance of the same resistors in parallel.

In a current divider the branch current is proportional to the OTHER branch's resistance: I₁ = I × R₂/(R₁ + R₂). Swapping the subscripts is the classic slip; check that the smaller resistor gets the larger current.

formulas.title: Series resistance
formulas.description: Total resistance of resistors carrying the same current; n equal resistors give nR.

formulas.title: Parallel resistance
formulas.description: Reciprocals (conductances) add for resistors across the same two nodes; n equal resistors give R/n.

formulas.title: Two resistors in parallel
formulas.description: Product-over-sum shortcut, valid for exactly two resistors; result is less than the smaller of the two.

formulas.title: Voltage divider
formulas.description: Voltage across R₁ when R₁ and R₂ are in series across supply V; drops are proportional to resistance.

formulas.title: Current divider
formulas.description: Current in R₁ when R₁ and R₂ are in parallel carrying total current I; the branch current is proportional to the other branch's resistance.

formulas.title: Cells in series and parallel
formulas.latex: E_s = nE,\; r_s = nr; \qquad E_p = E,\; r_p = \frac{r}{n}
formulas.plainText: Series: E_s = nE, r_s = nr ; parallel: E_p = E, r_p = r/n
formulas.description: n identical cells of EMF E and internal resistance r; series raises voltage, parallel raises current capacity.

flashcards.front: What happens to the total resistance when another resistor is added in parallel?
flashcards.back: It decreases — the equivalent of a parallel group is always less than its smallest member, because a new path (extra conductance) has been added.

flashcards.front: State the current-divider rule for two parallel resistors.
flashcards.back: I₁ = I × R₂/(R₁ + R₂): the current in a branch equals the total current times the other branch's resistance divided by the sum.

flashcards.front: Four 2 Ω resistors: equivalent resistance in series and in parallel?
flashcards.back: Series: 4 × 2 = 8 Ω. Parallel: 2/4 = 0.5 Ω.

flashcards.front: Why are household appliances connected in parallel rather than in series?
flashcards.back: Each appliance gets the full 230 V, can be switched on and off independently, and one failing does not stop the others — a series chain would break entirely.

questions.questionText: Resistors of 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 10 Ω are connected in series across a 40 V supply. The circuit current is:
An extra resistor is connected in series with an existing circuit across a fixed supply. The supply current:
questions.explanation: Adding a series resistor increases the total resistance, so I = V/R_total falls.

questions.questionText: The equivalent resistance of a 6 Ω resistor in parallel with a 12 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: R_p = (6 × 12)/(6 + 12) = 72/18 = 4 Ω, less than the smaller resistor as expected.

questions.questionText: Five identical resistors are connected first in series and then in parallel. The ratio R_series/R_parallel is:
questions.explanation: R_series = 5R and R_parallel = R/5, so the ratio is 5R ÷ (R/5) = 25 = n².

questions.questionText: Several resistors are connected in parallel across a fixed supply. The one that dissipates the most power is the resistor with the:
questions.explanation: All branches share the same voltage, so P = V²/R is greatest for the smallest R.

questions.questionText: A 24 V supply is connected across a 2 kΩ and a 6 kΩ resistor in series. The voltage across the 6 kΩ resistor is:
questions.explanation: V₆ = 24 × 6/(2 + 6) = 18 V; the larger resistor takes the larger share.

questions.questionText: A total current of 9 A enters a 3 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor connected in parallel. The current in the 3 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: I₃ = I × R_other/(R₁ + R₂) = 9 × 6/(3 + 6) = 6 A; swapping the resistances gives the wrong 3 A.

questions.questionText: Household appliances are connected in parallel across the supply mainly because:
options: The total current drawn is reduced
The same current flows through every appliance
Each gets the full supply voltage and can be switched independently
questions.explanation: In parallel every appliance sees the rated supply voltage, and switching or failure of one does not affect the others.

questions.questionText: A 2 Ω, a 3 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor are all connected between the same two terminals A and B. The resistance measured between A and B is:
An unknown resistor R in series with a 10 Ω resistor draws 2 A from a 50 V supply. The value of R is:
A 60 W, 230 V lamp and a 100 W, 230 V lamp are connected in series across a 230 V supply. Which statement is correct?
options: The 100 W lamp glows brighter because it has the higher rating
Both glow equally because the current is the same
The 100 W lamp glows brighter because it has the higher resistance
The 60 W lamp glows brighter because it has the higher resistance
questions.explanation: The 60 W lamp has the higher resistance (V²/P = 882 Ω against 529 Ω); with the same current in series, P = I²R is larger in the 60 W lamp.

questions.questionText: Two resistors have an equivalent of 25 Ω in series and 4 Ω in parallel. Their values are:
questions.explanation: R₁ + R₂ = 25 and R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = 4 give R₁R₂ = 100, so the values are the roots of x² − 25x + 100 = 0: 20 Ω and 5 Ω.

questions.questionText: Resistors of 10 Ω, 20 Ω and 30 Ω are connected in parallel across a 60 V supply. The total current drawn is:
questions.explanation: Branch currents are 60/10 = 6 A, 60/20 = 3 A and 60/30 = 2 A, totalling 11 A (1 A would be the series current).

questions.questionText: Three identical lamps are connected in parallel across a fixed supply and one of them burns out (goes open circuit). Then:
options: The other two also go out
The other two keep the same brightness and the supply current falls
questions.explanation: Each remaining lamp still has the full supply voltage, so its current and brightness are unchanged; only the burnt-out lamp's share of the supply current disappears.

questions.questionText: A 40 W, 220 V lamp and a 100 W, 220 V lamp are connected in series across a 220 V supply. Assuming constant lamp resistances, the power taken by the 40 W lamp is about:
questions.explanation: R₄₀ = 220²/40 = 1210 Ω and R₁₀₀ = 220²/100 = 484 Ω; I = 220/1694 = 0.130 A; P₄₀ = I²R₄₀ = 20.4 W (8.2 W is the 100 W lamp, 28.6 W the total).

questions.questionText: Ten identical lamps are connected in series across a fixed supply. If one lamp is short-circuited, the remaining nine lamps:
options: Glow dimmer, because the current falls
Glow brighter, because each gets a larger share of the supply voltage
questions.explanation: The total resistance falls from 10R to 9R, so the current rises and each remaining lamp's voltage rises from V/10 to V/9.

questions.questionText: A 100 V supply feeds two 10 kΩ resistors in series. A 10 kΩ load is connected across the lower resistor. The voltage across the load is about:
questions.explanation: 10 kΩ || 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ, so V_load = 100 × 5/(10 + 5) = 33.3 V; the unloaded divider would give 50 V.

questions.questionText: Which statement about a parallel circuit is NOT correct?
options: The equivalent resistance is greater than the largest branch resistance
The branch with the smallest resistance carries the largest current
The total conductance equals the sum of the branch conductances
Every branch has the same voltage across it
questions.explanation: Adding parallel paths lowers the resistance, so the equivalent is always less than the smallest branch; the other statements are true.

questions.questionText: A 2 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel combination of a 6 Ω resistor and a branch of two 3 Ω resistors in series. The network is connected to 20 V. The current in the 6 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: The 3 + 3 = 6 Ω branch in parallel with 6 Ω gives 3 Ω; total 2 + 3 = 5 Ω, so I = 20/5 = 4 A, which splits equally between the two 6 Ω paths: 2 A.

questions.questionText: What resistance must be connected in parallel with a 30 Ω resistor to give an equivalent of 12 Ω?
questions.explanation: 1/R = 1/12 − 1/30 = (5 − 2)/60 = 1/20, so R = 20 Ω (18 Ω is the simple difference, which is wrong for parallel).

questions.questionText: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, the element connected between the two midpoints of the bridge:
options: Carries no current and can be removed or shorted without changing the equivalent resistance
Must be replaced by a short circuit, otherwise the equivalent resistance is wrong
questions.explanation: At balance the two midpoints are at the same potential, so no current flows through the bridging element; removing it or shorting it gives the same equivalent resistance.

questions.questionText: n identical resistors of resistance R give 2 Ω in parallel and 50 Ω in series. Then:
questions.explanation: nR = 50 and R/n = 2; dividing gives n² = 25, so n = 5 and R = 10 Ω.

questions.questionText: A uniform wire of resistance R is cut into four equal pieces, and the pieces are connected in parallel. The resistance of the combination is:
questions.explanation: Each piece has R/4; four of them in parallel give (R/4)/4 = R/16.

questions.questionText: An ammeter is connected ____ with the load and should have a ____ resistance.
questions.explanation: The ammeter must carry the load current, so it goes in series, and its resistance must be very low so it does not reduce that current.

questions.questionText: A uniform wire of resistance 16 Ω is bent into a circle. The resistance between two points on the circle separated by a quarter of the circumference is:
questions.explanation: The two arcs are 4 Ω and 12 Ω in parallel: (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 3 Ω (4 Ω would be for diametrically opposite points).

questions.questionText: Six cells, each of EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are connected in series to a 7 Ω load. The terminal voltage of the battery is:
A 12 V battery and a 10 V battery, each with a small internal resistance, are connected in parallel with no load. What happens?
options: No current flows because there is no load
Each battery keeps its own terminal voltage and no current flows
A large circulating current flows from the 12 V battery into the 10 V battery
questions.explanation: The 2 V difference drives a current limited only by the two small internal resistances, discharging one battery into the other; this is why cells of unequal EMF are not paralleled.

questions.questionText: Four identical cells, each of EMF 2 V and internal resistance 0.4 Ω, are connected in parallel to a 1.9 Ω load. The load current is:
