questions.explanation: In parallel E = 2 V and r = 0.4/4 = 0.1 Ω, so I = 2/(1.9 + 0.1) = 1 A (0.87 A results from forgetting to divide r by 4).

questions.questionText: Identical cells are connected in parallel rather than in series mainly to:
options: Increase the current capacity while keeping the EMF of one cell
questions.explanation: Parallel cells keep the EMF of one cell but divide the internal resistance by n and add their ampere-hour capacities.

questions.questionText: Twelve cells, each of EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.6 Ω, are arranged in 3 parallel rows of 4 cells in series. The current in an external 2 Ω resistor is about:
questions.explanation: Each row has E = 4 × 1.5 = 6 V and r = 4 × 0.6 = 2.4 Ω; three rows in parallel give 6 V and 0.8 Ω, so I = 6/(2 + 0.8) = 2.14 A.

questions.questionText: Resistors of 10 Ω, 20 Ω and 30 Ω are in parallel across a battery. A wire of negligible resistance is accidentally connected across the 30 Ω resistor. The equivalent resistance becomes:
options: 6.67 Ω, the value of 10 Ω and 20 Ω in parallel
Zero, so the battery is short-circuited
questions.explanation: The wire is a 0 Ω branch in parallel with everything, and a parallel equivalent cannot exceed its smallest branch, so the whole combination becomes 0 Ω.

questions.questionText: Sixteen identical cells, each of EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 1 Ω, are to deliver the maximum current to an external 4 Ω resistor. The best arrangement is:
options: 4 parallel rows of 4 cells in series
8 parallel rows of 2 cells in series
2 parallel rows of 8 cells in series
questions.explanation: Maximum current needs nr/m = R with nm = 16: n/m = 4 gives n = 8, m = 2, so I = 12/(4 + 4) = 1.5 A, more than the 1.2 A given by 4 rows of 4 or by 16 cells in series.

questions.questionText: The rule that the total current in a parallel circuit equals the sum of the branch currents follows directly from:
questions.explanation: KCL states that the current entering a node equals the current leaving it, so the supply current equals the sum of the branch currents.

questions.questionText: A 10 Ω and a 40 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across a 20 V supply. The total power dissipated is:
questions.explanation: P = V²/R₁ + V²/R₂ = 400/10 + 400/40 = 40 + 10 = 50 W (8 W would be the series case).

questions.questionText: Resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω are in series across a 20 V supply. The power dissipated in the 5 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: I = 20/10 = 2 A, so P₅ = I²R = 4 × 5 = 20 W (80 W wrongly applies the full 20 V to the 5 Ω resistor).

questions.questionText: In a series circuit, the largest voltage drop appears across the:
questions.explanation: The same current flows through all, so each drop IR is proportional to the resistance.

questions.questionText: A resistor R is connected in parallel with a 6 Ω resistor, and this combination is in series with a 4 Ω resistor. The total resistance is 8 Ω. The value of R is:
questions.explanation: The parallel pair must equal 8 − 4 = 4 Ω, so 1/R = 1/4 − 1/6 = 1/12 and R = 12 Ω.

questions.questionText: To keep the output of a voltage divider close to its unloaded value when a load is connected, the load resistance should be:
options: Much smaller than the divider resistors
Equal to the lower divider resistor
Much larger than the divider resistors
questions.explanation: A load in parallel with the lower resistor lowers the effective resistance and the output; the effect is negligible only when the load is much larger (10 to 100 times) than that resistor.

questions.questionText: A meter movement of resistance 50 Ω gives full-scale deflection at 1 mA. The shunt needed to make it an ammeter reading 1 A full scale is about:
questions.explanation: The shunt carries 1 − 0.001 = 0.999 A at the same voltage as the meter (0.001 × 50 = 0.05 V), so R_sh = 0.05/0.999 = 0.050 Ω.

questions.questionText: A fuse is connected in series with the circuit it protects because:
options: It must have the full supply voltage across it
It raises the total resistance to limit the current
A series connection lowers its melting point
The whole circuit current passes through it, so it can interrupt that current when it melts
questions.explanation: Only a series element carries the full circuit current; when that current is excessive the fuse element melts and opens the one path the current has.

questions.questionText: A meter movement of resistance 500 Ω gives full-scale deflection at 1 mA. The series resistance needed to make it a 0 to 5 V voltmeter is:
questions.explanation: Total resistance = 5/0.001 = 5000 Ω, so the series multiplier = 5000 − 500 = 4500 Ω (5000 Ω forgets the meter's own resistance).

questions.questionText: A 6 V, 0.3 A lamp is to be run from a 12 V supply. The resistance to be connected in series with it is:
questions.explanation: The resistor must drop 12 − 6 = 6 V at 0.3 A: R = 6/0.3 = 20 Ω (40 Ω is the total circuit resistance).

questions.questionText: A bridge has arms of 2 Ω and 4 Ω in one path and 3 Ω and 6 Ω in the other, with a 10 Ω resistor connecting the two midpoints. The equivalent resistance between the supply terminals is:
questions.explanation: 2/4 = 3/6, so the bridge is balanced and the 10 Ω carries no current; R = (2 + 4) || (3 + 6) = (6 × 9)/15 = 3.6 Ω.

questions.questionText: Two resistors with conductances of 0.2 S and 0.3 S are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:
questions.explanation: Conductances add in parallel: G = 0.2 + 0.3 = 0.5 S, so R = 1/G = 2 Ω.

questions.questionText: The terminal voltage of a battery delivering current is less than its EMF because of:
options: The voltage drop across its internal resistance
The power factor of the load
The insulation resistance of the leads
questions.explanation: V = E − Ir: part of the EMF is used up driving the current through the battery's own internal resistance.

questions.questionText: Two 12 Ω resistors in series draw 1 A from a 24 V supply. A third 12 Ω resistor is then connected in parallel with one of them. The new supply current is:
questions.explanation: The parallel pair is 6 Ω, so R = 12 + 6 = 18 Ω and I = 24/18 = 1.33 A; the current rises because the total resistance fell.

subtopics.title: Star-Delta & Delta-Star Conversion
subtopics.subtitle: Δ→Y and Y→Δ formula sets, the balanced R_Y = R_Δ/3 case, and when to use them

concepts.text: Star and Delta Networks

Three resistors joined at a common point form a star (Y or T) network; three resistors joined in a closed loop form a delta (Δ, mesh or π) network. Both are three-terminal networks. Some resistor arrangements, such as a bridge, contain no purely series or parallel groups, so ordinary reduction stalls; replacing a delta by an equivalent star (or vice versa) creates series-parallel paths and the reduction can continue. The two networks are equivalent when the resistance measured between every pair of corresponding terminals is the same, so the external circuit cannot tell them apart.
Delta to Star (Δ → Y)

Let the delta have R_AB between terminals A and B, R_BC between B and C, and R_CA between C and A, and write S = R_AB + R_BC + R_CA for the sum of the three. The star resistance connected to any terminal equals the product of the two delta resistances that meet at that terminal divided by the sum S of all three delta resistances.

concepts.plainText: R_A = R_AB·R_CA / S ;  R_B = R_AB·R_BC / S

concepts.latex: R_C = \frac{R_{BC} R_{CA}}{S}, \qquad S = R_{AB} + R_{BC} + R_{CA}
concepts.plainText: R_C = R_BC·R_CA / S ;  S = R_AB + R_BC + R_CA

concepts.text: Star to Delta (Y → Δ)

Let the star have R_A, R_B and R_C connected to terminals A, B and C. The delta resistance between two terminals equals the sum of the two star resistances connected to those terminals plus their product divided by the third star resistance. An equivalent compact form uses the sum of pairwise products P = R_AR_B + R_BR_C + R_CR_A: each delta resistance is P divided by the star resistance at the opposite terminal, R_AB = P/R_C.

concepts.plainText: R_AB = R_A + R_B + (R_A × R_B) / R_C

concepts.latex: R_{BC} = R_B + R_C + \frac{R_B R_C}{R_A}, \quad R_{CA} = R_C + R_A + \frac{R_C R_A}{R_B}
concepts.plainText: R_BC = R_B + R_C + (R_B × R_C) / R_A ;  R_CA = R_C + R_A + (R_C × R_A) / R_B

concepts.text: Balanced (Equal-Resistance) Case

When all three resistances are equal the formulas collapse to a single factor of 3: a delta of three resistances R_Δ becomes a star of three resistances R_Y = R_Δ/3, and a star of three R_Y becomes a delta of 3R_Y. Star resistances are therefore the smaller ones. This is exactly the case for balanced three-phase loads, and it explains why a delta-connected load draws three times the power of the same resistors connected in star on the same line voltage.

concepts.plainText: R_Y = R_Δ / 3 ;  R_Δ = 3 × R_Y

rows: Product of the two adjacent Δ resistances ÷ sum of all three
Sum of two Y resistances + their product ÷ the third

concepts.text: When to use the conversion:
items: Unbalanced bridge networks (a Wheatstone bridge off balance), where no two resistors are simply in series or in parallel.
Finding the resistance between two points of a lattice, a cube of resistors or another symmetrical mesh.
Converting a delta-connected three-phase load to an equivalent star for per-phase analysis, and vice versa.
Simplifying T and π attenuator or filter sections — the same formulas hold for impedances in AC circuits.

concepts.text: Worked example: convert a delta with R_AB = 6 Ω, R_BC = 12 Ω and R_CA = 18 Ω to a star. S = 6 + 12 + 18 = 36 Ω. R_A = (6 × 18)/36 = 3 Ω, R_B = (6 × 12)/36 = 2 Ω, R_C = (12 × 18)/36 = 6 Ω. Check by converting back: R_AB = 3 + 2 + (3 × 2)/6 = 6 Ω, as given. Note that every star value is smaller than the delta values it came from.
Going Deeper: Star-Delta Conversion

The formulas come from one idea: with any one terminal left open, the resistance between the other two must be the same for both networks. With C open, the star shows R_A and R_B in series, while the delta shows R_AB in parallel with the path R_BC + R_CA. Writing this for all three terminal pairs gives three equations; adding two of them and subtracting the third isolates each star resistance.

concepts.plainText: R_A + R_B = R_AB (R_BC + R_CA) / (R_AB + R_BC + R_CA)

concepts.text: The Y→Δ formulas are easiest to remember in conductance form, where they look exactly like the Δ→Y resistance formulas: each delta conductance equals the product of the two star conductances at its ends divided by the sum of all three star conductances. This duality is also why balanced networks convert by the single factor 3 in both directions.

concepts.plainText: G_AB = G_A·G_B / (G_A + G_B + G_C), with G = 1/R

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - unbalanced bridge between A and B
A-C = 10 Ω, A-D = 20 Ω, C-D = 20 Ω, C-B = 12 Ω, D-B = 8 Ω
Balance test: 10/12 ≠ 20/8, so the C-D arm carries current
Convert delta ACD: S = 10 + 20 + 20 = 50 Ω
  Star arm at A = (10 × 20)/50 = 4 Ω
  Star arm at C = (10 × 20)/50 = 4 Ω
  Star arm at D = (20 × 20)/50 = 8 Ω
Path via C: 4 + 12 = 16 Ω   Path via D: 8 + 8 = 16 Ω
Parallel: 16 ∥ 16 = 8 Ω
R_AB = 4 + 8 = 12 Ω

Worked example 2 - star to delta with the compact form
Star: R_A = 3 Ω, R_B = 6 Ω, R_C = 9 Ω
P = R_A R_B + R_B R_C + R_C R_A = 18 + 54 + 27 = 99 Ω²
R_AB = P / R_C = 99/9 = 11 Ω
R_BC = P / R_A = 99/3 = 33 Ω
R_CA = P / R_B = 99/6 = 16.5 Ω
Check A-B (C open): 11 ∥ (33 + 16.5) = 544.5/60.5 = 9 Ω
Star gives R_A + R_B = 3 + 6 = 9 Ω  ✓

rows: A and B become one node
Only two resistors meet at C
R_AB open, R_BC = R_B, R_CA = R_A
C is the star point itself

concepts.text: Common mistakes to avoid:
items: Using the delta side opposite the terminal instead of the two sides that meet at it in Δ→Y.
Dividing by the star arm at one of the two terminals instead of the opposite one in Y→Δ.
Converting a delta whose resistors are not all joined to the same three nodes.
Applying R_Y = R_Δ/3 to capacitors: a capacitance triples, it does not divide by three.
Reporting a current through a resistor of the converted network as if it were a current in the original resistor.

concepts.text: Quick self-checks: every star arm must be smaller than both delta sides at its terminal, and R_A·R_BC = R_B·R_CA = R_C·R_AB after a Δ→Y conversion. Also, the terminal resistance with one terminal open must equal R_A + R_B for the star — test one pair before moving on.

Choose which triangle or star to convert so that the result produces series or parallel groups with the rest of the circuit. In a bridge, converting either end delta or the star at one of the middle nodes works; pick the one with the easiest numbers.

formulas.latex: R_{BC} = R_B + R_C + \frac{R_B R_C}{R_A}, \quad R_{CA} = R_C + R_A + \frac{R_C R_A}{R_B}
formulas.plainText: R_BC = R_B + R_C + R_B·R_C / R_A ;  R_CA = R_C + R_A + R_C·R_A / R_B

notes.text: Δ → Y: 'product of the two adjacent over the sum of all three' — the star resistance at a terminal uses the two delta resistors touching that terminal. Y → Δ: 'sum of two plus their product over the third' — the delta resistor between two terminals uses the two star resistors at those terminals, divided by the one opposite.
Do not reverse the factor 3: star resistances are SMALLER (R_Δ/3) and delta resistances are LARGER (3R_Y). If your star values come out bigger than the delta values, the formula has been inverted.

The conversion preserves every terminal-to-terminal resistance, so external currents and voltages are unchanged — but the currents inside the original network are lost. Convert back if a question asks for a branch current of the original delta or star.
For Y → Δ the compact form R_AB = (R_AR_B + R_BR_C + R_CR_A)/R_C saves arithmetic: compute the sum of pairwise products once and divide by the opposite star resistance for each side.

formulas.title: Delta to star: R_A
formulas.description: Star resistance at terminal A = product of the two delta resistances meeting at A divided by the sum of all three.

formulas.title: Delta to star: R_B and R_C
formulas.plainText: R_B = R_AB·R_BC / S ;  R_C = R_BC·R_CA / S
formulas.description: S = R_AB + R_BC + R_CA; same rule applied at terminals B and C.

formulas.title: Star to delta: R_AB
formulas.description: Delta resistance between A and B = sum of the star resistances at A and B plus their product over the third (opposite) star resistance.

formulas.title: Star to delta: R_BC and R_CA
formulas.latex: R_{BC} = R_B + R_C + \frac{R_B R_C}{R_A}, \quad R_{CA} = R_C + R_A + \frac{R_C R_A}{R_B}
formulas.plainText: R_BC = R_B + R_C + R_B·R_C / R_A ;  R_CA = R_C + R_A + R_C·R_A / R_B
formulas.description: Same rule for the other two sides of the delta; each uses the star resistance at the opposite terminal as divisor.

formulas.title: Star to delta (compact form)
formulas.latex: R_{AB} = \frac{R_A R_B + R_B R_C + R_C R_A}{R_C}
formulas.plainText: R_AB = (R_A R_B + R_B R_C + R_C R_A) / R_C
formulas.description: Sum of pairwise products of the star resistances divided by the star resistance opposite the side wanted; use R_A for R_BC and R_B for R_CA.

formulas.title: Balanced networks
formulas.description: When all three resistances are equal; star values are one third of delta values.

flashcards.front: Three 9 Ω resistors in delta: what star network is equivalent?
flashcards.back: Three 3 Ω resistors, since R_Y = R_Δ/3.

flashcards.front: State the delta-to-star rule in words.
flashcards.back: Each star resistance = (product of the two delta resistances meeting at that terminal) ÷ (sum of all three delta resistances).

flashcards.front: When is star-delta conversion needed?
flashcards.back: When a network, such as an unbalanced bridge, has no purely series or parallel groups; converting one delta (or star) creates series-parallel paths that can be reduced.

flashcards.front: What is unchanged when a delta is replaced by its equivalent star?
flashcards.back: The resistance between every pair of terminals, hence all external currents and voltages; the internal branch currents are not preserved.

questions.questionText: A delta network has R_AB = 10 Ω, R_BC = 20 Ω and R_CA = 30 Ω. The equivalent star resistance connected to terminal A is:
A star network has R_A = 2 Ω, R_B = 3 Ω and R_C = 6 Ω. The equivalent delta resistance R_AB between terminals A and B is:
A star network and a delta network are electrically equivalent when:
options: The resistance between each pair of terminals is the same for both
They contain the same number of resistors
The sum of all resistances is equal in both
Each network dissipates the same total power at no load
questions.explanation: Equivalence means the external circuit cannot distinguish the two networks, which requires equal resistance between every pair of corresponding terminals; the conversion formulas follow from this condition.

questions.questionText: A balanced star network has three 5 Ω resistors. Each resistance of the equivalent delta network is:
questions.explanation: For equal resistances R_Δ = 3R_Y = 3 × 5 = 15 Ω. (1.67 Ω results from dividing by 3 instead of multiplying.)

questions.questionText: A delta network has R_AB = 5 Ω, R_BC = 10 Ω and R_CA = 15 Ω. The equivalent star resistance connected to terminal C is:
questions.explanation: R_C = R_BC × R_CA / (R_AB + R_BC + R_CA) = (10 × 15)/30 = 5 Ω. The other values are R_A = 2.5 Ω and R_B = 1.67 Ω.

questions.questionText: A delta connection of three resistors is also known as a:
questions.explanation: Three resistors joined end to end in a closed loop form a delta, also called a mesh or π network; the star is the Y or T network.

questions.questionText: A star network has R_A = 4 Ω, R_B = 6 Ω and R_C = 12 Ω. The equivalent delta resistance R_BC between terminals B and C is:
questions.explanation: R_BC = R_B + R_C + R_B R_C / R_A = 6 + 12 + 72/4 = 36 Ω. (24 Ω is R_CA and 12 Ω is R_AB.)

questions.questionText: Three 8 Ω resistors are connected in star. The resistance measured between any two of its terminals is:
questions.explanation: Between two terminals the current passes through two star arms in series (the third arm is floating): 8 + 8 = 16 Ω.

questions.questionText: A delta network has R_AB = 20 Ω, R_BC = 30 Ω and R_CA = 50 Ω. The equivalent star resistance at terminal B is:
In a bridge network, A–C = 5 Ω, A–D = 10 Ω, C–D = 10 Ω, C–B = 6 Ω and D–B = 4 Ω. Using delta-star conversion of the delta ACD, the equivalent resistance between A and B is:
questions.explanation: Delta ACD (S = 25 Ω) gives star arms A = 5×10/25 = 2 Ω, C = 5×10/25 = 2 Ω, D = 10×10/25 = 4 Ω. Branches: 2 + 6 = 8 Ω and 4 + 4 = 8 Ω in parallel = 4 Ω; R_AB = 2 + 4 = 6 Ω.

questions.questionText: In a star (Y) network of three resistors:
options: The three resistors form a closed loop between the terminals
Each resistor is connected between one terminal and a common central point
All three resistors are in series between two terminals
All three resistors are in parallel across the same pair of terminals
questions.explanation: A star has one end of every resistor joined at a common (star or neutral) point and the other ends forming the three terminals; a closed loop is a delta.

questions.questionText: A star network has R_A = 1 Ω, R_B = 2 Ω and R_C = 3 Ω. Using the sum of pairwise products, the equivalent delta resistance R_CA is:
questions.explanation: P = R_AR_B + R_BR_C + R_CR_A = 2 + 6 + 3 = 11 Ω². R_CA = P / R_B = 11/2 = 5.5 Ω. (11 Ω is R_BC = P/R_A; 3.67 Ω is R_AB = P/R_C.)

questions.questionText: Star-delta transformation is mainly used to simplify a resistor network in which:
options: Some resistors are neither in series nor in parallel with each other
Only one voltage source is present
questions.explanation: Pure series or parallel groups can be combined directly; the conversion is needed when the connection (for example a bridge) blocks ordinary series-parallel reduction.

questions.questionText: A star network has R_A = 10 Ω, R_B = 10 Ω and R_C = 5 Ω. The equivalent delta resistance R_AB is:
questions.explanation: R_AB = R_A + R_B + R_A R_B / R_C = 10 + 10 + 100/5 = 40 Ω. Dividing by R_A instead of the opposite arm R_C gives the wrong 30 Ω.

questions.questionText: In each delta-to-star formula, the denominator is:
options: The product of all three delta resistances
The delta resistance opposite the terminal
The sum of all three delta resistances
The sum of the two delta resistances adjacent to the terminal
questions.explanation: R_A = R_AB R_CA / (R_AB + R_BC + R_CA); the same sum of all three delta resistances appears in every Δ→Y formula.

questions.questionText: A delta network has R_AB = 0 (terminals A and B shorted together), R_BC = 6 Ω and R_CA = 3 Ω. The equivalent star resistance at terminal C is:
questions.explanation: S = 0 + 6 + 3 = 9 Ω, so R_C = 6 × 3 / 9 = 2 Ω, while R_A = R_B = 0. This equals 6 Ω ∥ 3 Ω, as expected when A and B are the same node.

questions.questionText: A bridge network has A–C = 10 Ω, A–D = 30 Ω, C–D = 10 Ω, C–B = 6 Ω and D–B = 2 Ω. A 50 V DC source is connected between A and B. The current drawn from the source is:
questions.explanation: Delta ACD (S = 50 Ω) → star A = 10×30/50 = 6 Ω, C = 10×10/50 = 2 Ω, D = 30×10/50 = 6 Ω. Branches 2 + 6 = 8 Ω and 6 + 2 = 8 Ω in parallel = 4 Ω; R = 6 + 4 = 10 Ω, I = 50/10 = 5 A.

questions.questionText: In the star-to-delta formula R_AB = R_A + R_B + R_A R_B / X, the quantity X is:
options: R_C, the star resistance at the third terminal
questions.explanation: The delta side between A and B uses the two star arms at A and B and divides their product by the arm at the opposite (third) terminal C.

questions.questionText: A delta network has R_AB open-circuited (infinite), R_BC = 8 Ω and R_CA = 4 Ω. The equivalent star network is:
questions.explanation: With R_AB → ∞, R_A = R_AB R_CA/S → R_CA = 4 Ω, R_B → R_BC = 8 Ω and R_C = R_BC R_CA/S → 0. The network is simply 4 Ω and 8 Ω meeting at C.

questions.questionText: Three 30 Ω resistors are connected in delta. The resistance measured between any two terminals is:
questions.explanation: Between two terminals one 30 Ω side is in parallel with the other two in series: 30 ∥ 60 = (30 × 60)/90 = 20 Ω. The equivalent star (10 Ω arms) gives 10 + 10 = 20 Ω too.

questions.questionText: A delta network has R_AB = 12 Ω, R_BC = 18 Ω and R_CA = 6 Ω. The resistance measured between terminals A and B (C left open) is:
questions.explanation: R_AB side in parallel with R_BC + R_CA: 12 ∥ 24 = 288/36 = 8 Ω. Check with the star: R_A = 72/36 = 2 Ω, R_B = 216/36 = 6 Ω, R_A + R_B = 8 Ω.

questions.questionText: Three 9 Ω resistors connected in delta and three 6 Ω resistors connected in star are both joined to the same three terminals A, B and C. The resistance between A and B is:
questions.explanation: Convert the star to a delta of 3 × 6 = 18 Ω; each side is then 9 ∥ 18 = 6 Ω. Between two terminals of a 6 Ω delta: 6 ∥ 12 = 4 Ω.

questions.questionText: The star-delta conversion formulas can also be used in AC circuits provided:
options: Only the magnitudes of the impedances are used
Resistances are replaced by the complex impedances of the branches
questions.explanation: The derivation uses only the equality of terminal-to-terminal impedance, so the same formulas hold with complex impedances Z in place of R.

questions.questionText: A balanced three-phase load of three equal resistors draws 4 kW when connected in star to a supply. If the same three resistors are reconnected in delta on the same line voltage, the power drawn is:
questions.explanation: In delta each resistor gets the line voltage instead of V_L/√3, so each takes 3 times the power: P_Δ = 3 × 4 = 12 kW. Equivalently, the equivalent star of the delta has one third the resistance.

questions.questionText: Six 10 Ω resistors form the edges of a tetrahedron (every one of four nodes connected to every other). The resistance between any two nodes is:
questions.explanation: Between nodes 1 and 2 the network is a balanced bridge (the edge 3–4 carries no current): 10 ∥ (10 + 10) ∥ (10 + 10) = 10 ∥ 10 = 5 Ω. Delta-star conversion of any triangle gives the same result.

questions.questionText: Which of the following networks cannot be reduced using series and parallel combinations alone?
options: A ladder of resistors in series and parallel
Two resistors in parallel feeding a third in series
questions.explanation: In an unbalanced bridge the centre arm carries current and no two resistors are simply in series or parallel, so a Δ→Y (or Y→Δ) step is needed.

questions.questionText: A balanced delta-connected load of 60 Ω per phase is supplied at 400 V line voltage. Using its equivalent star, the line current is:
questions.explanation: Equivalent star R_Y = 60/3 = 20 Ω with phase voltage 400/√3 = 230.9 V, so I_L = 230.9/20 = 11.55 A (= √3 × 400/60). 6.67 A is the delta phase current.

questions.questionText: Three identical inductive reactances of j30 Ω are connected in delta. The equivalent star impedance per branch is:
questions.explanation: For identical impedances Z_Y = Z_Δ/3 = j30/3 = j10 Ω; the conversion keeps the inductive (+j) nature.

questions.questionText: A star network has conductances G_A = 2 S, G_B = 3 S and G_C = 5 S. The conductance G_AB of the equivalent delta is:
questions.explanation: In conductance form Y→Δ becomes 'product of the two adjacent over the sum': G_AB = G_A G_B /(G_A + G_B + G_C) = 6/10 = 0.6 S (R_AB = 1.67 Ω).

questions.questionText: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, the resistor connected across the detector arm:
options: Carries no current and can be removed without changing the equivalent resistance
Must first be converted to an equivalent star
Doubles the equivalent resistance of the bridge
questions.explanation: At balance both ends of the centre arm are at the same potential, so it carries no current; the bridge then reduces by series-parallel rules without any conversion.

questions.questionText: After a delta (R_AB, R_BC, R_CA) is converted to a star (R_A, R_B, R_C), which relation always holds?
options: R_A R_BC = R_B R_CA = R_C R_AB
R_A + R_B + R_C = R_AB + R_BC + R_CA
R_A R_AB = R_B R_BC = R_C R_CA
R_A = R_BC, R_B = R_CA, R_C = R_AB
questions.explanation: Each product equals R_AB R_BC R_CA / (R_AB + R_BC + R_CA), so a star arm multiplied by the delta side opposite it is the same for all three terminals — a quick check on the arithmetic.

questions.questionText: A delta network has Z_AB = 10 Ω (resistor), Z_BC = j10 Ω and Z_CA = −j10 Ω. The equivalent star impedance Z_C at terminal C is:
Star and delta networks that are to be interchanged must both be:
questions.explanation: The equivalence is between two three-terminal networks of three elements each; the resistance between each of the three terminal pairs must match.

questions.questionText: A star network with R_A = 3 Ω, R_B = 5 Ω and R_C = 7 Ω is converted to its equivalent delta. With terminal C left open, the resistance measured between A and B of the delta is:
questions.explanation: An equivalent network must give the same terminal resistance as the star: R_A + R_B = 3 + 5 = 8 Ω. (10.14 Ω is only the delta side R_AB, which is in parallel with R_BC + R_CA.)

questions.questionText: Twelve 12 Ω resistors form the edges of a cube. The resistance between two diagonally opposite corners of the cube (the body diagonal) is:
questions.explanation: By symmetry the current splits 3 ways, then 6 ways, then 3 ways: R = R/3 + R/6 + R/3 = 5R/6 = 5 × 12/6 = 10 Ω. (9 Ω is the face-diagonal value 3R/4, 7 Ω the edge value 7R/12.)

questions.questionText: A bridge has A–C = 10 Ω, A–D = 10 Ω, C–B = 8 Ω, D–B = 8 Ω and a 5 Ω resistor between C and D. The equivalent resistance between A and B is:
questions.explanation: The bridge is balanced (10/8 = 10/8), so C and D are at equal potential and the 5 Ω carries no current: R = (10 + 8) ∥ (10 + 8) = 9 Ω.

questions.questionText: When a delta is converted to a star, the star resistance at terminal A is calculated using the product of:
questions.explanation: R_A uses the two delta resistances that meet at terminal A, namely R_AB and R_CA, divided by the sum of all three.

questions.questionText: A delta inside a network is replaced by its equivalent star. Which quantity is generally NOT the same as in the original network?
options: The current entering each terminal of the delta
The voltage between any two terminals of the delta
The current and voltage of every element outside the delta
The current through each resistor of the original delta
questions.explanation: Only terminal behaviour is preserved; the currents (and powers) inside the removed delta must be found by going back to the original network.

questions.questionText: Three identical 30 µF capacitors are connected in delta. The capacitance per branch of the equivalent star is:
questions.explanation: Impedance rule Z_Y = Z_Δ/3. Since Z = 1/(jωC), a third of the impedance means three times the capacitance: C_Y = 3 × 30 = 90 µF. Dividing C by 3 wrongly treats C like a resistance.

questions.questionText: Compared with the two delta resistances that meet at its terminal, each resistance of the equivalent star is always:
questions.explanation: R_A = R_AB × R_CA/S and R_CA/S < 1, so R_A < R_AB; likewise R_A < R_CA. Star arms are always the smaller values.

questions.questionText: A star of three 4 Ω resistors is converted to a delta, and that delta is then converted back to a star. Each resistance of the final star is:
questions.explanation: Y→Δ gives 3 × 4 = 12 Ω and Δ→Y gives 12/3 = 4 Ω again — the two conversions are exact inverses.

questions.questionText: Which statement about star-delta equivalence is NOT correct?
options: The resistance between every pair of terminals is the same in both networks
The total power delivered to the network from outside is the same in both networks
The same formulas apply to complex impedances in AC circuits
The power dissipated in each individual resistor is the same in both networks
questions.explanation: Terminal behaviour, and therefore total input power, is identical, but the individual resistors differ in value and carry different currents, so their individual powers are not the same.

questions.questionText: A star of three 10 Ω resistors has an extra 15 Ω resistor connected directly between terminals A and C. The resistance between terminals A and B is:
questions.explanation: Star → delta of 30 Ω sides. Side CA becomes 30 ∥ 15 = 10 Ω. Between A and B: 30 ∥ (30 + 10) = 1200/70 = 17.14 Ω. (20 Ω ignores the 15 Ω; 8.57 Ω places it between A and B.)

questions.questionText: A star network has R_A = 6 Ω, R_B = 3 Ω and R_C = 0 (terminal C is the star point itself). The equivalent delta is:
options: R_AB = 9 Ω, R_BC = 3 Ω, R_CA = 6 Ω
questions.explanation: R_AB = R_A + R_B + R_AR_B/R_C → ∞ as R_C → 0, while R_BC = R_B = 3 Ω and R_CA = R_A = 6 Ω. A and B are already joined through C, so no direct side is needed.

questions.questionText: The delta-to-star formulas are derived by equating, for each pair of terminals with the third terminal open, the star resistance with the delta resistance. For terminals A and B this condition is:
options: R_A + R_B = R_AB (R_BC + R_CA) / (R_AB + R_BC + R_CA)
questions.explanation: With C open, the star gives R_A + R_B in series, while the delta gives R_AB in parallel with R_BC + R_CA. Writing the three such equations and solving them gives the Δ→Y formulas.

questions.questionText: A star with R_A = 2 Ω, R_B = 4 Ω and R_C = 4 Ω is converted to a delta. A 20 V source is connected between B and C of the delta, with A open. The current in the delta side R_BC and the source current are:
questions.explanation: Delta: R_AB = 2 + 4 + 16/4 = 8 Ω, R_BC = 4 + 4 + 16/2 = 16 Ω, R_CA = 8 Ω. I_BC = 20/16 = 1.25 A; total resistance 16 ∥ 16 = 8 Ω (= R_B + R_C), so the source current is 20/8 = 2.5 A.

questions.questionText: For per-phase analysis, a balanced delta-connected load of R ohms per phase on a line voltage V_L is replaced by an equivalent star in which each phase has:
questions.explanation: The balanced Δ→Y rule gives R_Y = R/3, and the star phase voltage is the line voltage divided by √3; the line current is then (V_L/√3)/(R/3).

questions.questionText: A star network has R_A = 5 Ω, R_B = 4 Ω and R_C = 12 Ω. Terminal C is connected directly to terminal B. The resistance between A and B is:
questions.explanation: With B and C joined, R_B and R_C are in parallel (4 ∥ 12 = 3 Ω) and in series with R_A: 5 + 3 = 8 Ω. The equivalent delta gives the same: P = 20 + 48 + 60 = 128, so R_AB = 128/12 = 10.67 Ω, R_CA = 128/4 = 32 Ω and R_BC = 128/5 = 25.6 Ω (shorted by the B–C link), giving R_AB ∥ R_CA = 10.67 ∥ 32 = 8 Ω.

questions.questionText: If every resistance of a delta network is doubled, the resistances of its equivalent star:
questions.explanation: Δ→Y resistances are (product of two)/(sum of three): doubling each value multiplies the numerator by 4 and the denominator by 2, so each star arm doubles.

concepts.text: How Circuits Are Classified

An electric circuit is a closed path through which current can flow, made of sources and elements joined by conductors. Circuits are classified in several independent ways: by the linearity of their elements, by whether their behaviour depends on the direction of current, by whether they can supply energy, by their size relative to the signal wavelength, by whether their parameters change with time, by the connection pattern and by the kind of supply. A single circuit belongs to one class in each pair — for example a resistor network fed by a battery is linear, bilateral, passive (apart from the source), lumped, time-invariant and DC.
Linear and Non-linear Circuits

A linear circuit contains only elements whose parameters (R, L, C) do not change with the applied voltage or current: the V-I graph is a straight line through the origin and the output is proportional to the input. Linear circuits satisfy homogeneity and additivity, so the superposition theorem, Thevenin's and Norton's theorems apply. A non-linear circuit contains elements whose parameters vary with V or I — diodes, transistors, iron-cored inductors near saturation, thermistors, arcs — giving a curved V-I graph; superposition does not hold and such circuits are analysed graphically, piecewise or numerically.
Bilateral and Unilateral Circuits

A bilateral element behaves identically for current in either direction — resistors, inductors and capacitors — so a network built from them, such as a passive filter or a transmission line, is bilateral. A unilateral element behaves differently for the two directions: a diode conducts one way and blocks the other; transistors, SCRs and vacuum tubes are also unilateral. A circuit containing any unilateral element is a unilateral circuit. The reciprocity theorem applies only to linear bilateral networks.
Active and Passive Circuits

Active elements can deliver energy to a circuit or amplify a signal: voltage and current sources (batteries, generators) and devices such as transistors and op-amps that need an external supply. Passive elements only absorb, store or dissipate energy — a resistor dissipates it as heat, an inductor stores it in a magnetic field and a capacitor in an electric field — and they can never provide power gain. A circuit with at least one energy source is an active circuit; one containing only R, L and C is passive. In the component classification used in electronics and in exam keys, semiconductor devices — diodes, transistors, ICs — are counted as active components and R, L, C as passive. Strictly, by the energy definition a diode cannot supply energy or amplify, so circuit theory treats it as a passive, non-linear, unilateral element; when an MCQ lists a diode beside R, L or C, the diode is the active one.

rows: Yes as a component (semiconductor); no gain by the energy definition

concepts.text: Lumped and Distributed Circuits

In a lumped circuit each element is treated as concentrated at a point and the connecting wires have zero impedance, so voltages and currents depend on time only. This is valid when the circuit is much smaller than the wavelength of the highest frequency present — at 50 Hz the wavelength is 6000 km, so all power and audio circuits are lumped. In a distributed circuit the resistance, inductance and capacitance are spread continuously along the length — a long transmission line, an antenna or a high-speed PCB trace — and voltages and currents vary with position as well as time, so per-unit-length parameters and wave equations are needed.
Time-invariant and Time-variant Circuits

A time-invariant circuit has element values that do not change with time, so a delayed input produces the same output, equally delayed — ordinary R, L, C networks with fixed values. A time-variant circuit has parameters that change with time: a potentiometer being turned, a switched-capacitor filter, a varactor whose capacitance follows a control voltage, or a modulator. Linear time-invariant (LTI) circuits are the ones to which phasor and Laplace analysis apply directly.
Open, Closed and Short Circuits; Connection and Supply
The three states a circuit path can be in:
items: Closed circuit: a complete path — current flows and the load works normally.
Open circuit: the path is broken (open switch, blown fuse, broken wire); R = ∞, I = 0, and the full source voltage appears across the gap.
Short circuit: a path of almost zero resistance bypasses the load; V ≈ 0 across it and the current is limited only by the source's internal resistance — dangerous, hence fuses and MCBs.
Series circuit: one path, same current everywhere. Parallel circuit: same voltage across every branch. Series-parallel circuit: a mixture, reduced step by step.

DC circuit: unidirectional steady current; in steady state only resistance matters (an inductor acts as a short, a capacitor as an open). AC circuit: alternating current (Nepal mains 230 V, 50 Hz); inductors and capacitors present reactance, so impedance, phase angle and power factor enter the analysis.

rows: Linear: R, L, C; superposition holds
Non-linear: diode, transistor; curved V-I graph
Bilateral: same both ways (R, L, C)
Active: contains a source, can amplify
Passive: only R, L, C; absorbs or stores

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Testing Circuit Types

To decide whether a circuit is linear, test its elements rather than its terminal graph. A practical source, an ideal source in series with a resistor, has the terminal line V = E − Ir, which does not pass through the origin, yet the circuit is still linear because every element obeys a proportional law. Superposition then applies to the independent sources: the response to all of them together is the sum of the responses to each one acting alone.

concepts.plainText: k(v1 + v2)² ≠ k·v1² + k·v2²  (square-law element fails additivity)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - a square-law element, I = 0.2 V²
3 V alone:  I = 0.2 × 9  = 1.8 A
2 V alone:  I = 0.2 × 4  = 0.8 A
Sum of separate responses = 2.6 A
Both together (5 V): I = 0.2 × 25 = 5 A  ≠ 2.6 A
Superposition fails: the element is non-linear
At 5 V: static R  = V/I = 5/5 = 1 Ω
        dynamic r = 1/(dI/dV) = 1/(0.4 × 5) = 0.5 Ω

Active and passive behaviour is decided with the passive sign convention: take the current as entering the element's positive terminal and compute p = v × i. A positive p means the element absorbs power at that instant; a negative p means it delivers power. A capacitor or inductor may deliver power for a while, but only energy it stored earlier, so its total absorbed energy never goes negative; an element whose total can go negative is active.

rows: Element absorbs power (acts as a load)
Element delivers power (acts as a source)
Total energy absorbed can be negative

concepts.plainText: θ = 360° × l/λ, λ = c/f  (electrical length)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2 - lumped or distributed? (c = 3 × 10^8 m/s)
(a) 300 km power line at 50 Hz
    λ = 3 × 10^8 / 50 = 6000 km
    θ = 360 × 300/6000 = 18°  -> long-line (distributed) model advisable
(b) 30 cm PCB trace carrying 100 MHz
    λ = 3 × 10^8 / 10^8 = 3 m
    θ = 360 × 0.3/3 = 36°  -> distributed (transmission-line) effects
(c) 2 m of house wiring at 50 Hz
    θ = 360 × 2/(6 × 10^6) ≈ 0.00012°  -> lumped
Common mistakes in classifying circuits:
items: Treating linear and bilateral as the same property: a thermistor is bilateral but non-linear.
Calling a circuit non-linear just because it contains an independent source; sources do not destroy linearity of the elements.
Deciding lumped or distributed from physical size alone: the test is size compared with wavelength, so it depends on frequency.
Confusing time-variant with non-linear: R(t) = 10 + 2t Ω is linear at each instant but changes with time.
Calling an inductor or capacitor active because it can release energy; it only returns what it stored.

rows: Any lumped circuit, linear or non-linear
Linear circuits (currents and voltages, not power)
Linear part of a circuit, seen from two terminals
Linear bilateral networks with a single source
Distributed circuits such as long lines

concepts.text: In DC steady state an inductor is a short and a capacitor an open, but only after the transient has died away. At the instant of switching the opposite is true: an uncharged capacitor behaves like a short and an inductor with no current behaves like an open.

For a classification MCQ, ask five quick questions in turn: Is there a source (active)? Are all elements proportional (linear)? Do any elements depend on direction (unilateral)? Is the circuit small compared with the wavelength (lumped)? Do any values change with time (time-variant)?

formulas.plainText: R = V / I (static) ;  r = dV / dI (dynamic)
Open circuit: R = ∞, I = 0 ;  Short circuit: R ≈ 0, V ≈ 0

notes.text: Labels to memorise: R, L and C are linear, bilateral and passive; a diode is non-linear and unilateral; a transistor is non-linear, unilateral and active. Most 'types of circuit' MCQs test exactly these labels.

Diode ambiguity: exam keys classify semiconductor devices (diode, transistor, IC) as active components and R, L, C as passive. By the strict energy definition a diode is passive because it cannot amplify. In an MCQ, pick the resistor, inductor or capacitor as the passive element.
Superposition, Thevenin, Norton and reciprocity require linearity, and reciprocity additionally requires bilateral elements. KCL, KVL and the maximum power transfer condition hold for any circuit.
Open circuit: I = 0 and the whole source voltage appears across the break. Short circuit: V ≈ 0 across the short and the current is very large. Fuses and MCBs protect against shorts, not opens.

formulas.title: Linearity (superposition) test
formulas.description: A circuit is linear when the response to a weighted sum of inputs equals the weighted sum of the individual responses (homogeneity plus additivity).

formulas.title: Static and dynamic resistance
formulas.plainText: R = V / I ;  r = dV / dI
formulas.description: For a linear element both are equal and constant; for a non-linear element (diode) the dynamic resistance dV/dI varies along the V-I curve.

formulas.title: Open and short circuit limits
formulas.plainText: Open: R = ∞, I = 0 ;  Short: R = 0, V = 0
formulas.description: Ideal limits used in analysis: an open carries no current, a short has no voltage across it.

formulas.title: Lumped-circuit condition
formulas.description: Circuit length l must be much smaller than the wavelength λ (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s); at 50 Hz λ = 6000 km, so power circuits are lumped.

formulas.title: Passivity condition
formulas.description: Total energy absorbed by a passive element is never negative; an active element can deliver net energy (w < 0).

flashcards.front: Is an inductor active or passive, and bilateral or unilateral?
flashcards.back: Passive (it stores energy in its magnetic field but cannot supply net energy or amplify) and bilateral (same behaviour for either current direction).

flashcards.front: Why is a diode called a unilateral element?
flashcards.back: Its behaviour depends on the direction of current: low resistance when forward biased, very high when reverse biased, so its V-I curve is not symmetric.

flashcards.front: What distinguishes a lumped circuit from a distributed one?
flashcards.back: In a lumped circuit the dimensions are much smaller than the signal wavelength, so elements act at points and quantities depend on time only; in a distributed circuit (long line, antenna) parameters are spread along the length and quantities vary with position too.

flashcards.front: Which network theorems fail in a non-linear circuit?
flashcards.back: Superposition, Thevenin's and Norton's theorems, because they require linearity; KCL and KVL still hold.

questions.questionText: The V-I characteristic of a linear resistor is:
options: A parabola starting at the origin
A straight line passing through the origin
questions.explanation: For a linear resistor V = IR with R constant, so V is proportional to I and the graph is a straight line through the origin whose slope is R.

questions.questionText: A linear resistive circuit gives an output current of 2 A when its input voltage is 5 V. If the input is raised to 12.5 V, the output current is:
questions.explanation: Linearity (homogeneity) means the output scales with the input: I = 2 × (12.5/5) = 5 A. 12.5 A would follow a square law, which a linear circuit cannot have.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a bilateral element?
questions.explanation: A capacitor behaves the same for either direction of current or polarity of voltage, so it is bilateral; diodes, SCRs and transistors are direction-dependent (unilateral).

questions.questionText: In a linear circuit, input x₁ alone produces an output of 3 mA and input x₂ alone produces −1 mA. The output when the input is 2x₁ + 3x₂ is:
questions.explanation: Homogeneity and additivity give y = 2(3 mA) + 3(−1 mA) = 6 − 3 = 3 mA. 2 mA ignores the weights; 9 mA ignores the minus sign.

questions.questionText: Which of the following elements is non-linear?
options: A metal-film resistor at constant temperature
An iron-cored inductor operating near magnetic saturation
questions.explanation: Near saturation the core permeability, and hence the inductance, falls as current rises, so the flux-current relation is curved; the other elements keep constant values.

questions.questionText: A silicon diode carries 10 mA with 0.7 V across it. Its static (DC) resistance at this point is:
questions.explanation: Static resistance R = V/I = 0.7 V / 0.01 A = 70 Ω. For a non-linear element this value changes with the operating point.

questions.questionText: A 12 V battery, a lamp and a switch are connected in series. With the switch open, the voltage across the switch terminals is:
questions.explanation: With the switch open no current flows, so there is no drop across the lamp and the full 12 V source voltage appears across the gap.

questions.questionText: A diode carries 10 mA at 0.70 V and 20 mA at 0.72 V. Its average dynamic (AC) resistance over this range is:
questions.explanation: r = ΔV/ΔI = (0.72 − 0.70)/(0.020 − 0.010) = 0.02/0.01 = 2 Ω. 70 Ω and 36 Ω are static values V/I at the two points.

questions.questionText: An ideal short circuit is connected across a load that is part of a working circuit. The voltage across the short circuit is:
questions.explanation: An ideal short has zero resistance, so V = I × 0 = 0 however large the current; the current is limited only by the rest of the circuit.

questions.questionText: Taking V_T = 26 mV, the dynamic resistance of a forward-biased silicon diode (ideality factor 1) carrying 2 mA DC is:
questions.explanation: r_d = V_T / I_D = 26 mV / 2 mA = 13 Ω. 350 Ω is the static value 0.7 V/2 mA.

questions.questionText: Taking the wave speed as 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the wavelength of a 50 Hz signal is:
questions.explanation: λ = c/f = (3 × 10⁸)/50 = 6 × 10⁶ m = 6000 km, far larger than any building wiring, so power circuits are treated as lumped.

questions.questionText: A 1 m length of cable carries a 300 MHz signal (wave speed 3 × 10⁸ m/s). Which statement is correct?
options: λ = 1 m, so lumped analysis is adequate
λ = 1000 m, so lumped analysis is adequate
λ = 0.1 m, so lumped analysis is adequate
λ = 1 m, so the cable is as long as a wavelength and distributed analysis is needed
questions.explanation: λ = c/f = 3 × 10⁸ / 3 × 10⁸ = 1 m. The lumped model needs l ≪ λ; here l = λ, so voltage and current vary along the cable and it must be treated as distributed.

questions.questionText: A circuit that contains at least one source of energy is called:
questions.explanation: A circuit with an energy source (battery, generator, or an amplifying device with its supply) is active; one with only R, L and C is passive.

questions.questionText: Using the passive sign convention, an element has 10 V across it and a current of 2 A that leaves its positive terminal. The element:
options: Delivers 20 W, so it is acting as a source (active)
Absorbs 20 W, so it is acting as a load (passive)
Delivers 5 W, so it is acting as a source (active)
Absorbs 20 W, so it is acting as a source (active)
questions.explanation: Current entering the + terminal means absorbed power; here it leaves, so p = v × i = 10 × (−2) = −20 W absorbed, i.e. 20 W delivered. Only an active element can deliver net power.

questions.questionText: In a distributed circuit, resistance, inductance and capacitance are:
options: Spread continuously along the length and specified per unit length
Constant with frequency and position by definition
questions.explanation: A distributed circuit, such as a long transmission line, has its parameters spread along its length (e.g. Ω/km, H/km, F/km), so quantities vary with position as well as time.

questions.questionText: An ideal inductor is a passive element even though it can return energy to a circuit. A 0.5 H inductor carrying 4 A can give back at most:
questions.explanation: Stored energy W = ½LI² = 0.5 × 0.5 × 16 = 4 J. It can return only what it has stored, which is why it is passive. 8 J forgets the ½ (LI²); 2 J (LI) and 1 J (½LI) use I instead of I².

questions.questionText: Which of the following must be treated as a distributed circuit rather than a lumped one?
options: A household lamp circuit at 50 Hz
The wiring of a car battery and starter motor
A microwave antenna operating at 3 GHz
questions.explanation: At 3 GHz the wavelength is only 10 cm, comparable with the antenna size, so its parameters must be treated as distributed; the other circuits are tiny compared with their wavelengths.

questions.questionText: A 12 V battery has an internal resistance of 0.05 Ω. If its terminals are accidentally short-circuited by a thick wire of negligible resistance, the current is:
questions.explanation: With a dead short only the internal resistance limits the current: I = 12/0.05 = 240 A — why short circuits are dangerous and need fuses or MCBs.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an example of a time-variant circuit?
options: A fixed 1 kΩ resistor connected to a battery
A circuit whose resistor value is being changed by a motor-driven potentiometer
A series RLC circuit with fixed component values
questions.explanation: A time-variant circuit has a parameter that changes with time; the continuously adjusted potentiometer does so, whereas the other circuits have fixed element values.

questions.questionText: The reciprocity theorem is applicable only to networks that are:
questions.explanation: Reciprocity (interchanging an ideal source and an ammeter leaves the reading unchanged) needs linearity and the same behaviour in both directions, so it applies to linear bilateral networks.

questions.questionText: In the steady state of a DC circuit, an ideal inductor and an ideal capacitor behave respectively as:
options: An open circuit and a short circuit
A short circuit and an open circuit
questions.explanation: At DC (f = 0) X_L = 2πfL = 0, so an inductor is a short, and X_C = 1/(2πfC) → ∞, so a capacitor is an open, once transients have died out.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can still be used to analyse a circuit that contains diodes?
options: Thevenin's theorem applied to the whole circuit
Norton's theorem applied to the whole circuit
questions.explanation: KCL and KVL follow from conservation of charge and energy and hold in any lumped circuit, linear or not; superposition, Thevenin and Norton require linearity.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a unilateral circuit?
questions.explanation: The half-wave rectifier contains a diode, which conducts in one direction only, so the circuit's behaviour depends on current direction; the others use only bilateral R, L and C.

questions.questionText: An NTC thermistor, whose resistance falls as the current through it heats it up, is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Its resistance depends on the current (through self-heating), so it is non-linear; it behaves the same in either direction (bilateral) and only dissipates energy (passive).

questions.questionText: A circuit in which the current always flows in one direction with a steady value is called:
questions.explanation: Direct current is unidirectional and, in steady state, constant; alternating current reverses direction periodically (50 Hz for Nepal mains).

questions.questionText: Which V-I relation describes a linear, bilateral resistor?
options: V = 5I for all values of I
V = 5I for I > 0 and V = 0 for I < 0
questions.explanation: V = 5I is a straight line through the origin (linear) and gives the same magnitude for either direction (bilateral). V = 5I² is non-linear; the piecewise law is unilateral.

questions.questionText: In the lumped-element model of a circuit, the connecting wires are assumed to have:
options: The same resistance as the load
questions.explanation: The lumped model places all R, L and C in the elements themselves and treats the interconnections as ideal conductors of zero impedance.

questions.questionText: The V-I characteristic of a bilateral element must be:
options: A straight line through the origin
Symmetrical about the origin, with the same shape in the first and third quadrants
Confined to the first quadrant only
questions.explanation: Bilateral means reversing the current reverses the voltage with the same magnitude, i.e. odd symmetry about the origin. A straight line is not required: a thermistor is bilateral but non-linear.

questions.questionText: Phasor and Laplace-transform methods apply directly to circuits that are:
questions.explanation: Both methods rely on superposition and on element values that do not change with time, i.e. on linear time-invariant (LTI) circuits.

questions.questionText: Even in a linear circuit with several sources, the superposition theorem cannot be used directly to find:
options: The power dissipated in a resistor
questions.explanation: Power is proportional to I² (or V²), which is not a linear function, so individual source powers do not add; find the total current or voltage first, then the power.

questions.questionText: A dependent (controlled) source used in the model of a transistor amplifier is classified as:
questions.explanation: A controlled source can deliver net power to the circuit — it represents the device's ability to amplify using its DC supply — so it is an active element.

questions.questionText: Which statement about passive elements is NOT correct?
options: A passive element can deliver more energy to the circuit than it has previously absorbed
A resistor converts all the electrical energy it absorbs into heat
An ideal capacitor can return the energy stored in its electric field
An ideal inductor stores energy in its magnetic field
questions.explanation: The total energy absorbed by a passive element, w(t) = ∫vi dt, is never negative, so it can never deliver more than it has taken in. The other statements are correct.

questions.questionText: A bridge rectifier fed from the 230 V, 50 Hz mains and supplying a resistor is:
options: Linear and bilateral, with a DC supply
Non-linear and bilateral, with an AC supply
Linear and unilateral, with an AC supply
Non-linear and unilateral, with an AC supply
questions.explanation: The diodes make the circuit non-linear (curved V-I) and unilateral (direction-dependent); the supply is AC even though the load current is unidirectional.

questions.questionText: An air-cored 0.1 H inductor is used first on a 50 Hz AC supply and then on a steady DC supply. Its reactance in the two cases is:
options: 31.4 Ω at 50 Hz and infinite at DC
5 Ω at 50 Hz and 0 Ω at DC
31.4 Ω at 50 Hz and 0 Ω at DC
0.0318 Ω at 50 Hz and 0 Ω at DC
questions.explanation: X_L = 2πfL = 2π × 50 × 0.1 = 31.4 Ω; at DC f = 0 so X_L = 0 and only the winding resistance limits the current.

questions.questionText: A 10 Ω and a 20 Ω resistor are in series across a 30 V DC supply. If the 20 Ω resistor becomes short-circuited, the supply current becomes:
questions.explanation: Normally I = 30/30 = 1 A. With the 20 Ω shorted only 10 Ω remains: I = 30/10 = 3 A.

questions.questionText: Three 30 Ω resistors are connected in parallel across a 30 V supply. If one resistor goes open-circuit, the total supply current becomes:
questions.explanation: Each branch takes 30/30 = 1 A regardless of the others, so the total falls from 3 A to 2 A; the remaining branches are unaffected because the voltage across them is unchanged.

questions.questionText: A string of identical lamps is connected in series across 230 V. One lamp filament breaks. Which statement is correct?
options: All lamps go out; about 230 V appears across the broken lamp and 0 V across each good lamp
Only the broken lamp goes out; the others stay lit
All lamps go out; 0 V appears across the broken lamp and 230 V is shared among the good lamps
All lamps stay lit at reduced brightness
questions.explanation: The break makes an open circuit, so I = 0 everywhere: the good lamps have no drop (V = IR = 0) and the full supply voltage appears across the gap.

questions.questionText: A non-linear element obeys I = 0.01V² (I in A, V in V). At V = 10 V, its static resistance and dynamic resistance are respectively:
questions.explanation: I = 0.01 × 100 = 1 A, so R = V/I = 10 Ω. dI/dV = 0.02V = 0.2 S, so r = dV/dI = 1/0.2 = 5 Ω. The two differ because the element is non-linear.

questions.questionText: A linear circuit has two independent voltage sources. With V₁ = 10 V acting alone the load current is 2 A; with V₂ = 5 V acting alone it is 1.5 A (same direction). The load current when V₁ = 20 V and V₂ = −10 V act together is:
questions.explanation: Scale each response: V₁ doubled → 2 × 2 = 4 A; V₂ = −2 × 5 V → −2 × 1.5 = −3 A. Superposition: 4 − 3 = 1 A. 7 A ignores the sign reversal of V₂.

questions.questionText: A resistor's value varies with time as R(t) = 10 + 2t Ω (t in seconds). A constant 2 A flows through it. The voltage at t = 10 s and the correct classification are:
questions.explanation: R(10) = 10 + 20 = 30 Ω, so V = 2 × 30 = 60 V (it was 40 V at t = 5 s for the same current). V is still proportional to I at each instant (linear), but R changes with time (time-variant).

questions.questionText: A PCB is to be analysed as a lumped circuit, which requires its 15 cm length to be no more than one tenth of the wavelength. Taking the wave speed as 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the highest signal frequency allowed is:
questions.explanation: λ must be at least 10 × 0.15 = 1.5 m, so f ≤ c/λ = (3 × 10⁸)/1.5 = 2 × 10⁸ Hz = 200 MHz. 2 GHz is the frequency at which λ equals the board length.

questions.questionText: A 24 V source with 0.2 Ω internal resistance supplies an 11.8 Ω load. If the load terminals are short-circuited, the current and its ratio to the normal load current are:
options: 2 A, the same as the normal current
2.03 A, about 1.02 times the normal current
questions.explanation: Normal current = 24/(0.2 + 11.8) = 2 A. With the load shorted only 0.2 Ω remains: I = 24/0.2 = 120 A, which is 120/2 = 60 times larger.

questions.questionText: A 400 km overhead line operates at 50 Hz (take the wave speed as 3 × 10⁸ m/s). Its electrical length, 360° × l/λ, is:
questions.explanation: λ = (3 × 10⁸)/50 = 6000 km, so l/λ = 400/6000 = 0.0667 and θ = 360 × 0.0667 = 24°. A phase shift this large is why long lines are modelled with distributed parameters.

questions.questionText: A non-linear element obeys I = 0.5V² (I in A, V in V). Sources of 2 V and 4 V are connected in series aiding across it. The actual current, and the current superposition would wrongly predict, are:
questions.explanation: Actual: V = 6 V, I = 0.5 × 36 = 18 A. Superposition would add 0.5 × 4 = 2 A and 0.5 × 16 = 8 A to get 10 A — wrong, because the element is non-linear.

questions.questionText: A 1 m long circuit contains a 230 V, 50 Hz source and a fixed resistor, air-cored inductor and capacitor. Which classification is correct?
options: Active, linear, bilateral, lumped, time-invariant AC circuit
Passive, linear, bilateral, distributed, time-invariant AC circuit
Active, non-linear, unilateral, lumped, time-variant AC circuit
Active, linear, bilateral, lumped, time-invariant DC circuit
questions.explanation: The source makes it active; fixed R, air-cored L and C are linear and bilateral; 1 m ≪ 6000 km makes it lumped; fixed values make it time-invariant; the supply is AC.

questions.questionText: A 12 V DC source is connected through a 4 Ω resistor to an ideal inductor, and a capacitor is connected directly across the inductor. In the steady state, the current from the source and the capacitor voltage are:
questions.explanation: In DC steady state the inductor is a short circuit, so I = 12/4 = 3 A, and the capacitor, being across that short, has 0 V. 0 A and 12 V would treat the inductor as open.

questions.questionText: A 10 V DC source feeds a 2 Ω resistor in series with two parallel branches: one is a 3 Ω resistor in series with a capacitor, the other an 8 Ω resistor. In the steady state, the source current and the capacitor voltage are:
questions.explanation: In steady state the capacitor is open, so its branch carries no current: I = 10/(2 + 8) = 1 A. No drop occurs across the 3 Ω, so V_C equals the 8 Ω voltage, 1 × 8 = 8 V.
